Draft spec · v0.9 · 2026-11-05

Software Factory

A cloud service that never stops. It watches one or more Scrum backlogs, takes Product Backlog Items one at a time or several in parallel, and runs each through a written SOP with Claude agents. Every item that meets the Definition of Done ships as an Increment.

Yours you asked for it My call a default you can override All decisions logged in §14

01Intent

Refined, ordered backlog items sit waiting for a developer to free up. The factory takes the routine ones, so people spend their time refining the backlog and reviewing and accepting work.

Throughput and quality are measured together. The factory is working when its Increments pass the same Definition of Done as human work, cost per item is one the team accepts, and people spend less time per item than they would building it themselves.

02Scope

Goals

  • Runs in the cloud 24/7. Yours
  • A private dashboard for reporting and monitoring. Yours
  • Watches backlogs, picks PBIs, runs the SOP, delivers an Increment. Yours
  • Concurrency is a fixed number or comes from past cadence. Yours
  • Any orchestration decision can be overridden from the dashboard. Yours
  • BDD and TDD by default. Behaviour is written in Gherkin at planning, and every test fails before the code that makes it pass. Yours
  • PRs are tiered Low, Medium or High risk and need 0, 1 or 2 human approvals, the model Anthropic's Claude Code team uses. Yours
  • Every run is auditable, down to the SOP version, model and cost. My call

Non-goals

  • Writing or ordering the backlog. The Product Owner keeps that. My call
  • Running Sprint events. The factory feeds Sprint Review and nothing more. My call
  • Production deploys in v1. The factory stops where your Definition of Done stops, staging at most. My call

Anti-goals

The factory has failed, even if it runs, when it:

  • merges work a human reviewer would have rejected,
  • touches items or repos nobody gave it,
  • adds to human review load,
  • spends money it can't account for item by item.

03Scrum terms the factory uses

The factory follows the 2020 Scrum Guide. Two passages set its delivery rule.

"The moment a Product Backlog item meets the Definition of Done, an Increment is born."Scrum Guide 2020, Commitment: Definition of Done, scrumguides.org
"Multiple Increments may be created within a Sprint. ... However, an Increment may be delivered to stakeholders prior to the end of the Sprint."Scrum Guide 2020, Increment

So the factory never holds work for the end of a Sprint. Each PBI that passes the DoD gate becomes an Increment right then. At Sprint Review, the team presents the sum of that Sprint's Increments.

TermWhat it means in the factory
PBIOne work item in a connected backlog, either a GitHub Projects item or an Azure DevOps work item. It is eligible only when it carries the opt-in label, factory by default. My call
ReadyThe Scrum Guide has no formal "Ready". It says only that items which can be Done within one Sprint are "deemed ready for selection". So each repo writes its own Definition of Ready in .factory/dor.md, and the factory checks every item against it. The engine itself checks only the rules listed under "What stays in the engine" in §6, plus the opt-in label. An item that fails gets a comment listing the lines it failed and stays in the backlog. See Policy files in §6. Yours
Definition of DoneThe repo's own .factory/dod.md, so each repo can have a different one. The factory adds one line of its own: every scenario passes on main. The cell checks each line before the PR opens, a person ticks the lines left for them, the factory merges only once every one is ticked (PBI 181), and stage 10 confirms the factory's own line on main. Yours
IncrementThe merged change and its evidence: PR link, DoD results, the scenario runs from before and after the code, and a release note line. Recorded per PBI, rolled up per Sprint. The feature files stay in the repo as living documentation of what the product does.
ScenarioOne Gherkin Example, tied to an acceptance criterion by a tag such as @ac-2. Scenarios are the contract between the Product Owner and the factory. Once signed off, the build can't change them. Yours for Gherkin, My call for the lock.

04Architecture

There are two planes. A small control plane runs all the time. Work cells start once per PBI and shut down when it finishes. Only the control plane runs 24/7, which keeps idle cost low. My call

ComponentJobNotes
Backlog watcherMirrors eligible items from each backlog into the state store.Takes webhooks where the backlog system sends them, and polls every 5 minutes to catch missed events. Each backlog system gets its own adapter, described below. My call
Readiness gateDecides whether an item can enter.The engine's own checks run first. Then a cheap model judges the item against the repo's dor.md, line by line. It comments on items and edits none, except a parent whose split it files, which loses its opt-in label, and a child it filed that fails dor.md lines, whose body it rewrites once (PBI 264, §6). For an item the judge reports too big for one Sprint, the gate also asks the SOP's coding model to propose a split, once per item text, and files a valid one as child items (§6, "Policy files"). My call
SchedulerStarts a cell when a WIP slot frees up.Follows backlog order. Takes the top ready item and skips any whose dependencies aren't Done. See §7.
Work cellRuns one PBI through the SOP in an isolated sandbox.Fresh clone, its own branch, a token for one repo, a budget cap. Saves a checkpoint after every stage so a crashed cell can resume.
State storeThe one source of truth for items, runs, stages, costs and WIP policy.Postgres. Every state change is also appended to an event log, which feeds the dashboard and the audit trail. My call
DashboardReporting, monitoring and a few controls.See §8.

Backlog and repo adapters

GitHub ships first. Azure DevOps and other systems plug in later without changes to the scheduler, SOP runner or dashboard. Yours The core talks to two interfaces, one for backlogs and one for repo hosts. They're separate because a team can keep its backlog in one system and its code in another.

InterfaceCallsFirst adapter
BacklogList eligible items since a cursor, get one item, claim and release, comment, set status, link a PR, close an item, and turn a webhook payload into a factory event.GitHub Projects
Repo hostClone and push a branch, open, update and close a PR, request reviewers, read review state and mergeability, post the risk-approval status check, read approvals with the commit each covers, and read branch protection.GitHub
  • One shape inside. The core only sees factory items, events and states. Each backlog source's config maps its own fields to them: where acceptance criteria live, which status values mean Queued or Done, which label or tag opts an item in. A new board layout needs config, not code. My call
  • Contract tests. One shared test suite that every adapter must pass, plus an in-memory fake adapter that the rest of the factory's tests run against. A new adapter is done when it passes the suite. My call
  • Declared capabilities. Each adapter states what its system supports, webhooks for example. The watcher polls when a system has no webhooks. My call
  • Next in line. Azure DevOps Boards and Azure DevOps Repos in Phase 3. Jira, Linear or any other system follows the same path.

05PBI lifecycle

Every item moves through one state machine, and its state lives only in the state store. The backlog item mirrors it through a status field and comments, so people who never open the dashboard can still follow along.

 stateDiagram-v2 [*] --> Eligible Eligible --> NotReady: readiness check fails NotReady --> Eligible: item edited, or a readiness input changed Eligible --> Abandoned: label removed, or item closed NotReady --> Abandoned: label removed, or item closed Abandoned --> Eligible: label back or re-queued, after a withdrawal from Eligible or NotReady NotReady --> Split: split filed, last child filed and label off Abandoned --> Split: split filed before PBI 225, every child among its sub-issues Split --> Done: every filed child Done Eligible --> Queued: ready Queued --> InProgress: WIP slot + claim InProgress --> SignOff: scenarios written SignOff --> InProgress: approved, or changes asked InProgress --> NeedsInput: agent blocked NeedsInput --> InProgress: answered, by a person, or by the factory once CI passes on the base or the PR conflicts or gets a new review, or its question from before PBI 292 names only CI failures InProgress --> InReview: PR open, CI green InReview --> Queued: changes requested, or a conflict InReview --> Accepted: approvals met, or merged by the factory or a person InProgress --> Accepted: merged during address NeedsInput --> Accepted: merged by the factory or a person while waiting Accepted --> Done: DoD verified after merge, or main green again after a merge onto a red main InProgress --> Failed: retry budget spent NeedsInput --> Abandoned: no answer in 5 days SignOff --> Abandoned: no answer in 5 days InProgress --> Queued: lease expired, or a usage limit Accepted --> Failed: DoD fails after merge, bug PBI filed Failed --> Queued: human re-queues Failed --> Accepted: re-check finds the merge no longer broke main Abandoned --> Queued: re-queued, or a late answer Abandoned --> SignOff: re-queued, sign-off still open Abandoned --> NeedsInput: re-queued, question still open, PR not closed Done --> [*]
  • Claiming. The scheduler takes a lease on the item and the cell renews it every 60 seconds. After 5 missed renewals the lease expires and the item goes back to Queued, branch intact. Every attempt of the item's run still marked started is then closed as stopped, ending at that moment, with a message saying the cell's lease ran out, so a dead cell's attempt never stays open. A restart that sends a cell's item back to Queued closes them the same way. Like any stopped attempt, such an attempt uses up none of the stage's retries (PBI 239). Each lease carries a generation number that goes up on every claim, and again whenever the item leaves InProgress. A cell checks its generation before every push, comment and state write, and exits once it no longer holds the lease. It also stops itself after 3 minutes of failed renewals, before the 5-minute expiry, so an old cell is gone before a new one starts. My call
  • Needs input. The agent posts its question as a comment on the item and in the dashboard. You answer in either place. On the item, a comment that starts with /answer counts, and only when its GitHub login maps to a user on the dashboard's allowlist, so ordinary discussion on the item is never taken as an answer. The item gives up its WIP slot while it waits, so one stuck item can't stall the line. The factory reminds on the item and on Floor at day 2 and day 4, and after 5 days with no answer the item is Abandoned. My call
  • Sign-off. Scenarios wait for the Product Owner the same way. On the item, a product owner comments /approve, or /changes followed by a note. The sign-off view lists each acceptance criterion beside the scenarios tagged with it and flags any criterion with none. Above the buttons it also shows a Scope section with the issue's body as written on GitHub, and every feature file up for sign-off in full, as it stands at the scenarios sha, so the owner can judge the scenarios against the work without opening GitHub. An empty body shows no Scope section. A timed-out item that can still be signed off shows the same view. Reminders and the 5-day limit work as for Needs input.
  • Waiting on people. An item that waits for a person holds no slot, so the WIP number alone doesn't bound the work landing on people. In every concurrency mode the scheduler starts no new item while the items waiting on a person reach review_capacity, default 3. Those are items whose question or sign-off is still unanswered, plus factory PRs waiting on a reviewer. An item whose answer has arrived can always resume, so answering never stalls the line. A priority-1 item, its own priority or one it inherits, gets past this brake too, so what matters most is never kept waiting by it, as #305 and #317 were on 2026-11-15 (PBI 320). Floor shows the count beside the WIP number. My call
  • Claim order. Every item has a priority from 1 to 5, where 1 is the highest, read from the board's Priority field on each poll. A missing value, or one that isn't a whole number from 1 to 5, counts as 3. An item is final-stage while its PR is open and it's in the review loop: InReview, at address, or at the PR review that follows address. Every final-stage item is in one group, whichever of those stages it's in. The scheduler claims Start now first, then the final-stage group, then every other item, and within each group by priority, 1 first. Within one priority the order is as before: answered items first, then the factory queue's order, which Move up and Move down change. An item that a final-stage item depends on, directly or through other items, joins the final-stage group with that item's priority, wherever it is in the pipeline, so it's picked up to unblock its dependent. Outside the group, an item that a higher-priority item depends on takes that priority. Either way the item goes back to its own group and priority once the dependency is gone, or once the item depending on it is Done or otherwise finished. Floor and Run detail show each item's priority and whether it's final-stage, and name the item either one comes from when it isn't the item's own. The priority isn't judged and doesn't re-gate an item, unless the repo lists Priority as a readiness field: then dor.md can refer to it like any other readiness field, and setting or changing it sends the item back through the readiness check. A priority-1 item still never gets past a hold, an open blocker or the readiness gate (PBI 320). My call
  • Coming back. A Failed or Abandoned item returns to Queued when an operator re-queues it, and an Abandoned item also returns when its question gets a late answer. An item that failed its Definition of Done on main also returns to Accepted on its own when a re-check finds the merge no longer broke main, as Red main in §10 describes (PBI 369). An item withdrawn from Eligible or NotReady never passed the readiness gate, so a re-queue sends it back to Eligible to meet the gate instead (PBI 168). It resumes at its last checkpoint, except when its PR has already merged; then it starts a new run on a new branch. When a person closed its PR without merging, it resumes at Open PR, which opens a fresh PR from the same branch. A merge or a close that happens while the item is In progress, during address for example, or while it waits in Needs input after its PR opened, counts the same way: the webhook, or the poller when no webhook came, moves the item to Accepted or withdraws it. A move to Accepted from Needs input closes the open question, so the dashboard stops asking for an answer, and a Needs input item whose PR is still open keeps waiting (PBI 194) unless the factory merges it under stage 10's rules (PBI 262). An address run that found no trusted review text and no conflict used to ask "no trusted review text to address", before PBI 258 made it pass instead, and an item may still wait on that question. Once the poller reads that item's PR as conflicting with its base, or a trusted review or a comment in a still-open thread newer than the question asks for changes, the factory answers the question itself, naming the conflict or the review and its time and naming nobody as the one who answered, and logs the re-queue as a system event. The item is then claimed again at address. A person's answer, a Hold or an earlier poll that got there first wins, a held item is re-queued only once it's released, and an item waiting on any other question still waits for a person (PBI 305). An item that asked the older "Address failed" question before a CI failure went back to Green (PBI 292), that is before PR #309 merged at 2026-11-15T05:50:19Z, is answered the same way once every finding the question names is a CI failure: the answer says the factory sends the item back to Green to fix the CI failure, names nobody as the one who answered, and the re-queue is a system event. The item is then claimed again at Green. The claim merges the base, as every claim does, and Green's findings are the failed checks of the PR's head as it is now, each with its URL and failing tests. A question that names anything besides CI failures still waits for a person, and a person's answer, a Hold or an earlier poll that got there first wins. So does the same question asked since then, which is address giving up after CI failed on each of its own fixes: that run stopped before it posted its thread replies, so only a person's answer, which reruns address, gets them posted, and a re-queue to Green would skip address and leave the reviewer's threads unanswered (PBI 317). A cell that reaches Open PR, or starts an address run, on a branch whose PR has already merged opens nothing, calls no agent and ends the stage as failed, naming the merged PR. Address asks before it merges the base, so a squash-merged branch never conflicts its way into a question. A stage that waits for CI on its push, Open PR, address or PR review, may find the factory refusing to say whether CI passed, because a person merged the PR meanwhile and the commit is gone from the branch or now on main. The stage then asks for the PR's state. A merged PR ends it the same way, naming the merged PR, and one closed without a merge ends it naming the closed PR, for the poller to withdraw the item. Neither asks anyone, runs another attempt or moves the item. A refusal while the PR is still open fails the attempt as before, so a cell can't learn CI on a commit that isn't its own (PBI 212). An item re-queued while its question is still open goes back to waiting, with a fresh 5-day clock, unless a person closed its PR without merging: then the question closes and the item resumes at Open PR, so the next poll doesn't withdraw it again over the same closed PR (PBI 194).
  • Backlog changes. The watcher compares each item in the factory with the version the run started from. When the acceptance criteria change, the factory comments on the item, closes its PR if one is open, and starts a new run from Understand on a new branch from the base, which leads to a new sign-off. A fresh branch matters because the old one already holds code, so new scenarios would pass before Red. When the opt-in label is removed or the item is closed, the factory stops the run, frees the slot, closes the factory's PR with a comment, keeps the branch and moves the item to Abandoned. An Eligible or NotReady item that loses its label or closes is withdrawn to Abandoned the same way, on the next poll and before the readiness gate sees it, so it leaves Floor's "Not ready" list. It has no run, so there's nothing to stop or close. If such an item gets its label back, it returns to Eligible on the next poll and meets the readiness gate again, so it never reaches Queued without passing it. An item withdrawn from Queued or later stays Abandoned when its label comes back (PBI 168). A Split parent stays Split when it loses its label, gets it back or closes, since its work goes on in its children (PBI 225). Its one way out is to Done, once every child the factory filed for it is Done (PBI 226). A parent split before PBI 225 lost its label once its split was filed and was withdrawn to Abandoned. Each poll first moves such a parent to Split, once, before it could return to Eligible: an Abandoned item withdrawn from Eligible or NotReady with a split kept for it, and every child of that split among its sub-issues by its split marker. It then reaches Done like any Split parent. An Abandoned item with no kept split, or one abandoned any other way, stays Abandoned (PBI 228). All of these moves are logged as system events. My call
  • Board status. The factory owns the status field of the items it holds. The project's built-in workflows that set status, such as item closed and pull request merged, stay off. A factory PR references its item with Refs #n, so a merge doesn't close it, and the factory closes the item when it reaches Done. Yours
  • Assignment. While an item is in the factory, it's assigned to the factory's bot account, so no person picks it up at the same time. Where the git host can't assign the bot, a factory:in-progress label does the same job.
  • Overrides. A dashboard override can move an item along paths the diagram doesn't draw, such as holding a queued item or sending a reviewed one back to Specify. Each such move is logged as an override event. See §8.

06SOP

You said the SOP is still to be defined. The factory treats it as data, a versioned file in a repo. Each run pins the SOP version of the cell image on its first claim. A cell image holds only one SOP, so when a run pinned to an older version resumes, it moves to the image's SOP and carries on from the stage it was at. The run records the new version, and the factory logs the move as a system event on the item. The one run that can't move is one whose next stage the image's SOP lacks. That run asks for input, and the question names the stage. Below is a v0 to start from. It works outside in. Gherkin scenarios define the behaviour at planning and must fail first. Unit tests then drive the code inside each scenario, and the scenarios pass last. Review uses the agents you already run.

#StageWhoExit gateOn failure
1UnderstandPlanner agentRestates each acceptance criterion and tags it @ac-1, @ac-2 and so on. Lists the files likely to change. Stops at Needs input if a criterion can't be tested.Needs input
2SpecifyPlanner agentGherkin feature files committed to the branch, written to the repo's scenarios.md. Every criterion has at least one tagged scenario, the files parse in the runner, and the scenarios are posted on the PBI. A short plan names the unit tests expected under each scenario.Retry once, then Needs input
3Sign-offProduct OwnerApproves the scenarios on the PBI or in the dashboard. The factory then locks the feature files at that commit. YoursRequested changes go back to stage 2
4RedBuilder agentStep definitions written, plus stubs for the entry points the When steps call. A stub returns an empty or default value and holds no behaviour, so the When runs and the Then fails. A stub never replaces behaviour a @regression scenario relies on. Every scenario the repo's bdd.run selects, except a @regression one, runs and fails on an assertion, never on an undefined step or a crash. A scenario bdd.run leaves out, such as an @local one, runs on the owner's machine instead, so Red doesn't expect it. A @regression scenario passes, as "Red proof" below says. See "Reading runner results" below. The failing run is kept as evidence, and the feature files match the lock.Retry up to 2 times, then Needs input
5GreenBuilder agentTDD inside each scenario: a failing unit test, the least code that passes it, then refactor. Exits when every scenario and the full unit suite pass, lint and type check are clean, the feature files still match the lock, and no dod.md line failed.Retry up to 3 times
6Self-reviewself-reviewerReports APPROVED, or OPEN: 0, which says the same. Its brief is the repo's pr-review.md, plus the engine's BDD checks: every step definition asserts something, no scenario is pending or skipped, and no tag hides a scenario from the run. The builder fixes or rebuts each finding and sends it back, the same loop your CLAUDE.md sets for every PR.A finding still held after 2 rebuttals, or no approval after 5 rounds, goes to Needs input
7Open PRBuilder agentPR references the PBI with Refs #n. The body starts with the agent's summary, which must open with a ## Problem section. The factory drops the agent's chatter first: a summary wrapped in a fenced block keeps only the fence's contents, and text before its first ## heading is left out. A wrapper that opens with a markdown or md info string, or none, closes at the first fence-only line that leaves no code block inside it open, so code blocks inside it are kept (PBI 291) and a note after it, with its own code block, is left out (PBI 297). When a fence-only line could close the wrapper or open a bare code block inside it, and a ## heading after it only counts if it opens one, the line opens a bare code block if a later fence-only line then closes the wrapper with no code block inside it open, so a wrapped body with a bare code block before more sections reaches the PR whole (PBI 291). A line spaced as a closing fence, with text right before it and a blank line after it, gives the finding below instead, since a bare code block that starts with a blank line is spaced the same as a wrapper's end before a note whose code block holds a ## line, and closing the wrapper there could silently drop the sections after that block (PBI 297). With no such heading, the line's spacing decides: text right before it and a blank line after it closes the wrapper, and a blank line before it and text right after it, with its block's closing fence spaced as one, opens a bare code block, so a bare code block with text after it in the body's last section is kept whole too (PBI 291). When no such line closes the wrapper, or the spacing fits both readings, the factory can't tell where the body ends, so the attempt fails with a finding that says so, and the retry asks for the body alone (PBI 297). A body that leaves a code block open fails the attempt, and the retry asks for the body alone (PBI 291). A summary that still doesn't start with ## Problem fails the attempt, and the retry asks for the body alone (PBI 216). The body lists each scenario with its red and green result and states the review rounds. CI green.CI failures go back to stage 5. Green's findings name each failed check, its URL and the tests it names as failing, read from the failed GitHub Actions job's log, and a check whose log names no test, or one the factory can't read, is named with its URL alone. Green's findings also carry the last 100 lines of each failed check's log, which the cell API reads from the repo host, so the cell needs no GitHub access to learn why CI failed. The repo host reads logs for the first 5 failed checks only, the ones the finding shows a log for, and gives every later check a null log, so a run with many failed checks doesn't download logs nobody reads. Each log line is cut at 500 characters, and the oldest lines go once the log passes 20,000 characters, so a large dump can't swell the finding (PBI 232). While Green fixes it, its attempt is reported as fixing CI, with the commit and the failed checks, and Floor and Run detail show that. The cell never reads CI again on a head CI already failed on, so no attempt is charged twice for one failure. When Green leaves that commit unchanged, CI has nothing new to judge, and the item goes to Needs input instead of Failed. Green running out of retries still fails the item. The question names each failed check with its URL and failing tests, each commit CI failed on, and how many times Green tried. Before it goes back to Green, the cell reads CI on the base commit, origin/<base>. When every failed check names failing tests and the base's failed checks fail each of them too, the base is at fault: the stage asks the base question of PBI 215, naming each check with its URL, and never sends the item to Green (PBI 292). A summary that doesn't start with ## Problem, or an agent call that fails, gets 1 retry, then goes to Needs input (PBI 216). CI still pending 60 minutes after the cell began waiting on a commit goes to Needs input, with a question naming each check still pending. A timeout isn't a CI failure, so it never goes back to stage 5 or uses up a retry, and each commit gets its own 60 minutes (PBI 234)
8PR reviewpr-reviewer, pr-addresserpr-reviewer reviews the PR's head against the repo's pr-review.md before any person is asked to look, while the item is still In progress. The factory posts each review as one review at the commit it reviewed, with one line comment per finding. Before it posts, it reads the PR's diff at that commit, and a finding on a line outside it goes in the review's summary instead, as a bullet naming its path:line and its text, since GitHub turns down the whole review for one line it can't place. A summary finding is a new finding like any other: pr-addresser answers it in the same round, its reply goes on the PR as a comment that quotes it, and the reviewer checks it on the next round. The stage's message names each finding moved to the summary and why (PBI 266). pr-addresser answers the findings in the same cell, by a fix or a reply on the thread, and the reviewer checks each of its threads at the new head. The factory resolves a thread the reviewer finds fixed, or whose reply it accepts. A held thread stays open, with a reply naming what still fails. The stage passes when a review brings no new finding and none of the factory's threads is open, and the PR body then states its rounds. Only then does the factory request reviewers and move the item to In review. A person's thread is never one of the factory's. Each claim that reaches the stage starts by reading the PR's open review threads, and every one the factory's reviewer opened is the stage's own, with its conversation so far, whichever claim opened it. Only the factory's own replies make up that conversation: a reply someone else left inside the thread never reaches the reviewer or the addresser. So a thread an earlier claim left open is checked again at the new head, holds the stage open until it's resolved, and counts in the review's "earlier threads still open". Round numbers carry on from the last round any earlier claim posted on the PR (PBI 318). The stage runs again in the same cell after pr-addresser answers a person's review, once CI passes on what it pushed, and the item returns to In review only when that review passes (PBI 130). A thread the factory's own review opened, one whose first comment is by the repo's trusted bot, belongs to this stage, so it never sends the item back to address, through the webhook or the poller, even when a trusted person replies inside it. A review requesting changes counts only when it has a summary or a comment outside those threads, so a reply in one submitted as Request changes sends nothing either. Whether a person's thread sends the item back depends only on whether it is unresolved when the poller reads it, never on what its comments say, and an approval with a summary sends nothing back. Each changes_requested event names its cause: the review or thread comment and when it was submitted, or that GitHub reported the PR not mergeable (PBI 258). Once address has dealt with a person's thread, by a fix CI has passed on or a reply it posted, the factory resolves that thread. A thread address only marks fixed, when it committed nothing since it started, has no fix CI could pass on, so it stays unresolved unless address also replied in it. A thread it didn't answer stays unresolved. Before resolving, it reads the threads again, and a thread that gained a comment since the claim, other than its own reply, stays unresolved too, because address never read that comment and the poller sends the item back for it. An address run with no trusted review text and no merge conflict asks nothing: it passes, and this stage hands the PR back once its review passes (PBI 258). The webhook can't see a review's line comments, so it leaves a review with no summary to the poller. A person's review counts from the moment the cell records the PR, so one left while this stage runs, with the item still In progress, sends it back to address on the first poll after it reaches In review (PBI 191). An address run whose PR a person has already merged ends without blocking or asking, before it merges the base, and leaves the item for the poller or the webhook to move to Accepted (PBI 194). A merge or a close while the stage waits for CI on the addresser's fix ends the stage as failed, naming the PR, with no further attempt, question or move of the item, as "Coming back" describes (PBI 212). A Needs input item waiting on "no trusted review text to address" goes back to address on a conflict or a newer trusted review too, as "Coming back" describes (PBI 305). A Needs input item waiting on an "Address failed" question asked before #292 that names only CI failures goes back to Green to fix the CI failure on the PR's head, as "Coming back" describes. The same question asked by address since then still waits for a person, whose answer reruns address and posts its thread replies (PBI 317). Branch current with base. Stage 9 counts human approvals once it has set the tier.CI failing on the addresser's fix goes back to stage 5, counted against its retries. CI failing on what address pushed when the addresser made no commit, such as its merge of the base when the addresser only replied, goes back to stage 5 too: address has no agent work left to change that commit, so it doesn't retry on it. In that case it posts its replies, and the run goes back to Green with the failed checks as at stage 7 (PBI 292). Either way Green's findings name each failed check, its URL and the last lines of its log, with the same caps as at stage 7, read through the cell API (PBI 232). CI failing on a fix the addresser committed in address is retried there, as before. CI still pending on a fix 60 minutes after the cell began waiting on it, here or in address, goes to Needs input as at stage 7 (PBI 234). A finding still held after 2 replies, or no clean review after 5 rounds, goes to Needs input, naming the open threads. A review GitHub still turns down with a 422 is posted once more with every finding in its summary and no line comment, and only a second 422 goes to Needs input, naming each finding, since the same review would fail every claim (PBI 266). An answer the stage can't read gets one restate in the same reviewer session, which doesn't count against the stage's retries, and one still unreadable goes to Needs input with the restated answer's reason (PBI 190)

Example feature file

What stage 2 produces for a PBI with two acceptance criteria:

@pbi-482 Feature: Export invoices to CSV Finance exports one month of invoices to reconcile them in a spreadsheet. Rule: Only invoices dated in the chosen month are exported @ac-1 Scenario: Invoices from other months are left out Given invoices dated 2026-10-31, 2026-11-01 and 2026-12-01 When finance exports November 2026 Then the file contains 1 invoice And that invoice is dated 2026-11-01 Rule: Amounts keep their currency @ac-2 Scenario Outline: Amount and currency are separate columns Given an invoice for <amount> <currency> When finance exports that invoice's month Then the row shows "<amount>" under Amount and "<currency>" under Currency Examples: | amount | currency | | 120.50 | AUD | | 99.00 | USD |

BDD rules

  • Traceability. Every acceptance criterion gets a tag, and at least one scenario carries it. Stage 2 fails on any criterion without a scenario. Each feature file also carries its PBI's tag, such as @pbi-482. Red and the traceability check look only at that PBI's scenarios, and the lock covers only its files. Green runs the whole suite, so earlier Increments' scenarios keep guarding against regressions.
  • Business language. Scenarios describe behaviour the Product Owner can read, with no selectors, SQL or class names. Implementation detail belongs in step definitions. This rule, and a Rule per business rule with scenarios for the happy path, edge cases and failures, make up the default scenarios.md. A repo can replace them. The other rules in this list belong to the engine.
  • The lock. At sign-off the factory records the commit of the feature files. After that the build may add step definitions and unit tests, but it may not edit, skip or tag out a locked scenario. Every later gate compares the feature files against the lock. Every agent that works after sign-off is told which feature files are locked. When a stage's work changes one anyway, the factory restores the locked files to the lock commit, commits that, names the restore in the attempt's findings and carries on, so the next attempt or round starts from the signed-off scenarios. At red, green and address the attempt fails and retries. Self-review and open-pr carry on with the restored files. The owner is never asked about it, since no answer would change the files. The self-reviewer holds no finding open for a scenario change. A scenario it thinks is wrong goes in the PR body as a note for the person who merges. The run keeps those notes, so a PR body written in a later claim, after a usage limit, a stop, an answered block or a requeue, still carries them. A scenario that turns out wrong goes back to Specify and through sign-off again. My call
  • Red proof. A scenario that passes before any behaviour exists tests nothing new, or its steps don't assert. Stage 4 reports it as a finding and doesn't proceed. A scenario tagged @regression is the exception. It restates behaviour that already holds, such as "every existing test still passes", so Red needs it green instead, and a red or crashed one is the finding. An item whose every scenario is @regression fails Red, because Red then proves nothing. Red expects only the scenarios the repo's bdd.run selects with its own tag filter, such as --tags "not @local". The factory learns which those are by running bdd.run with --dry-run added, since cucumber-js reports a test case only for a scenario its filter selects, wherever the filter is set: in the command, in a profile, in an environment variable, or in an npm script the command runs with a trailing --. The added flag has to reach cucumber-js: npm run <script> keeps a trailing --dry-run for npm unless the command already passes --, and a trailing || true or pipe sends it elsewhere. So Red checks that the report really comes from a dry run, with no step that ran, and fails with a finding that says so when it doesn't, rather than read a real run, which leaves out a selected scenario that didn't run, as the list of what bdd.run selects. A scenario bdd.run leaves out runs on the owner's machine instead. So a scenario that filter leaves out doesn't count against Red, while one it selects that doesn't run fails Red as not run in the cell. An item none of whose scenarios bdd.run selects fails Red, since nothing then proves it red. Traceability still counts every scenario, filtered or not. Green treats @regression like any other scenario.
  • Runners. Each repo uses its existing Gherkin runner. Cucumber lists official implementations for JavaScript, Java, Kotlin, Ruby, Scala and C++ (cucumber.io). For .NET, Reqnroll is "a Cucumber-style BDD test automation framework" built as "a reboot of the SpecFlow project" (reqnroll.net). A repo with no runner gets one in its first factory PBI, and its commands go in the repo config. My call
  • Reading runner results. Every runner writes a Cucumber Messages report, the format the Cucumber project calls "the preferred standard" (cucumber/messages). Reqnroll writes it from v3.0 (Reqnroll formatters). The factory reads step statuses from that report and never parses console output. A scenario counts as red only when its first non-passing step is FAILED and is an Outcome step, a Then. Any UNDEFINED, PENDING or AMBIGUOUS step, a failed hook, or a failure in a Given or When counts as a crash. A missing or empty report gives no verdicts, so Red fails every expected scenario as not run, and Green fails too (schema). My call

Risk tiers

Stage 9 copies the approval model from "How the Claude Code team does code review" (claude.dev, 2026-10-15). The table is theirs, word for word. Yours The approvals column is the engine's. The examples column is the default risk.md, and a repo replaces it with its own examples of what each tier means there.

RiskExamplesHuman approvals
LowDocs, copy, internal-only features, additive changes behind a flagNone required once automated review and security checks are green
MediumOrdinary product changes, and changes to sensitive areas such as caching, the auto-updater, or system promptsOne person
HighThe highest-risk code, plus a small set of paths that always need two peopleTwo people
  • The change sets the tier. A classifier reads the diff and the repo's risk.md, and picks the tier, whoever or whatever wrote it. A second pass asks whether this particular change needs a person even when its tier says no. Path rules run first, and no risk.md can lower them. CI workflow files, the repo's sensitive_paths, anything under .factory/ or .claude/, and AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md anywhere in the repo always need at least one person. Those files steer the factory's own agents, so a change to them must never pass at Low. The classifier uses the coding model, because a wrong Low lets code skip review. My call for the model.
  • Agents never fill a human slot. Approvals from self-reviewer, pr-reviewer or any other agent don't count toward the number. A Low PR merges without a person only once automated review and the repo's security checks are green.
  • Trusted authors. In the source, only authors on a repo's trusted list get the lighter paths, and everyone else needs a second person. The factory's bot account is treated as an author like any other. It gets the table's numbers only in repos whose owners add it to the trusted list. Elsewhere a factory PR needs one more person than its tier says, up to two. Yours for per-repo trust, My call on how to read "a second person".
  • No directing person. In the source, whoever prompted an agent counts as one of its reviewers. A factory item has no such person, so every required approval comes from a reviewer.
  • One commit per approval. An approval covers the commit it was given on. When the factory pushes after an approval, for example pr-addresser fixing a thread or resolving a conflict, the approval no longer counts and the factory asks again. One exception keeps stage 8's base syncs from adding review load. An approval still counts when every commit since it is a merge of the base that leaves the PR's diff unchanged. The factory checks that by comparing the patch-id of git diff base...head at the approved commit and at the new head.
  • Enforcement. Low needs zero approvals, so the git host can't require a fixed review count. The factory posts a required status check, risk-approval, that turns green only when the tier's approvals are met on the head commit. Branch protection requires that check with the factory's GitHub App as its expected source. GitHub then blocks the merge "if the status is set by any other person or integration" (GitHub). The App has no admin rights and is on no bypass list, so it can't change the protection that checks it.
  • Review requests. Once the PR review stage passes, the factory requests reviewers from the repo's CODEOWNERS file, or from reviewers in .factory/config.yml when the repo has no CODEOWNERS. Floor shows how long each PR has waited. My call
  • Visible tier. The PR body and the dashboard show the tier and the classifier's reasons, so a reviewer can challenge them. An operator can raise a tier. Nothing lowers one, overrides included.

Policy files

The factory is generic. Its engine owns the mechanics: states, leases, the scenario lock, red proof, approval counting and path floors. Every judgement about what is good enough lives in plain markdown in the repo's .factory/ folder, in the team's own words. The factory reads each file at the run's pinned commit and hands it to the agent or model that makes that judgement. Yours

FileDecidesRead byIf the repo has none
dor.mdDefinition of Ready: whether an item can enterReadiness gateFactory default: testable criteria, a clear scope, one Sprint's work
scenarios.mdHow scenarios are written and how deep they goSpecifyFactory default: the business-language rules in BDD rules below
pr-review.mdWhat a review checksself-reviewer in stage 6, pr-reviewer in stage 8, and linked in the PR body for peopleFactory default: correctness, security, what the linked item asks for, and the repo's own AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md or CONTRIBUTING.md
risk.mdWhat Low, Medium and High mean in this repoRisk classifier in stage 9Factory default: the examples column of the Risk tiers table
dod.mdDefinition of DoneThe cell at the end of Green, and the PR body's checklistNone. The team owns its Definition of Done, so a repo without one fails readiness
  • Two kinds of file. dor.md, pr-review.md and dod.md hold criteria. Each top-level checklist line, - [ ], is one criterion. The factory numbers the criteria and reports on each as passed, failed or, in dod.md only, left for the person who merges, with a reason. A missing answer counts as a fail. scenarios.md and risk.md are guidance. The agent that writes scenarios, or picks a tier, reads the whole file, and nothing scores them line by line. Prose in any file is guidance. My call
  • Who judges. In dor.md the readiness model judges each line against the item text and its readiness fields. In pr-review.md the reviewer judges each line against the diff, and stage 6 passes only when it reports APPROVED, or OPEN: 0, which says the same, and every line passed. In dod.md an agent in the cell judges each line against the diff, the scenario report and CI, before the PR opens. A line it can't decide before merge, such as "deployed to staging", it marks for the person who merges. That line goes to the PR checklist unticked and never fails the item. A person ticks the checklist at merge. Self-review and review fixes can push code after that check, so the cell checks dod.md again before the PR opens or returns to review whenever the branch head has moved, and the checklist names the commit it was checked at.
  • Commands. Only dod.md may hold a line with run: <command> in backticks. The cell runs it in the repo checkout before the PR opens, with a 15-minute limit and an env holding only PATH, HOME, CI=true, the proxy variables, and FACTORY_PG_BIN when the image sets it, so a test can start its own Postgres. The line passes only when the command exits 0. That env keeps the cell's tokens out of the command's variables, but the command runs as the cell's own user. So it has the same reach as the repo's test command and as the agent that wrote the code, and no more. A run: line in any other file makes that file invalid, and the factory reports why. When a line's command fails, the cell runs the same command on the run's base commit, origin/<base>, in a worktree of its own, before it charges the failure to the item. That run is a plain command, with no AI call, and happens only after a line has failed. If every test that failed on the item's branch fails on the base too, the stage doesn't retry. It asks one question that says the base fails in the cell and names the failing tests and the base commit, so a person can see the item isn't at fault. Before it asks, the cell commits the work in progress and pushes it to the item's branch, so the stage runs again on that work once the base is fixed. It checks its lease first and pushes nothing if that check fails, and it never pushes a commit that changed a locked feature file. The question says the work is on the branch only when that push happened. A failure only the item's branch has is handled as before, with retries (PBI 215). Once CI passes on a newer commit of the base branch, and no newer commit's CI has failed, the factory answers each such question itself, naming the commit CI passed on, and logs the re-queue as a system event. The item is claimed again at the stage it stopped at, and that claim merges the base, as every claim does, so a conflict that arose while it waited is resolved then. An item on Hold is re-queued only once it's released, and an item waiting on any other question still waits for a person (PBI 260). My call
  • CI checks. A dod.md line can also name a CI check, as ci: <check name> in backticks, such as ci: ci. Running the full suite in the cell again repeats work CI has already done on the same commit. So once the item has a PR, the cell asks the control plane which checks CI reported on the commit it is judging. When the named check passed there, the line passes, with the check's name and URL as its reason, and the cell doesn't run the line's command. When it failed, the line fails the same way. Only a check of exactly that name on exactly that commit counts. A check on an earlier commit stands in for nothing. When there is no PR, as at green, or CI hasn't reported on the commit, or the check is still running, the cell runs the line's command or judges the line as it did before. A named check that CI didn't run on a commit it did report on also falls back, and the stage's findings say the check was missing, so a misnamed check shows up and doesn't fail the line by itself. A ci: line outside dod.md makes that file invalid, as a run: line does. My call
  • Defaults. The factory ships each default under policy/ in its own repo, inside both its images. A repo file replaces the default whole and never merges with it, so what a team reads is what runs. A file falls back to its default only when the repo truly lacks it. A failed read stops that step and retries, because silently swapping a team's stricter file for the default would be worse. Run detail says which files came from the repo and which were defaults. The worker reads each default from the commit of main it last fetched into the operator's checkout, the commit it builds the cell image from, for both the readiness fingerprint and the gate's criteria, never from the checkout's working tree or local commits. So a default policy change merged to main re-checks every NotReady item on the next poll, as a change to a repo's own policy file does, with no restart of the worker or the control plane and no restart notice on Floor, and an edit nobody merged counts for nothing. When a fetch fails, the defaults stay those of the commit last fetched. Cells keep reading the defaults baked into their image (PBI 261). My call
  • What stays in the engine. This is the one list of rules no policy file can weaken. A file can add criteria on top.
    • An item needs at least one acceptance criterion, a known repo, valid factory config and a dod.md. An open dependency doesn't fail it: the gate queues the item blocked by the issues it waits on, and the scheduler takes it up only once they close (PBI 237). When the caller knows the factory's App lacks a permission it needs on the repo, each one it lacks fails the item, and the readiness comment says the owner has to grant it (PBI 264).
    • The readiness check flags item text that asks for credentials, CI changes or access outside the repo.
    • The readiness check reports whether an item is too big for one Sprint. It comes from the engine's judge prompt, as the flags do, so no dor.md can remove it.
    • The scenario lock, red proof and @pbi scoping.
    • The review's BDD checks: every step definition asserts something, no scenario is pending or skipped, and no tag hides a scenario. They outrank anything in pr-review.md.
    • The path floors.
    • Agents never fill a human slot, and the approval count per tier.
    • A dod.md line left for the person who merges raises the PR to at least Medium, so a person is there to check it.
    • The factory's own DoD line: every scenario passes on main.
    • The self-review and address stages run the factory's own reviewer and addresser, whatever agent files the checkout holds. "One rubric" below gives the mechanism.
    My call
  • Coding standards. There is no policy file for them. Build agents already load the repo's own AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md, so a team writes its conventions where its people already look. Because those files steer the agents too, they sit inside the path floor.
  • One rubric. The vendored self-reviewer and pr-reviewer keep only their review loop and report format. Their rubric comes from pr-review.md alone. The cell carries them under factory-only names, such as factory-self-reviewer. Claude Code prefers a repo's .claude/agents/ over the user's when two agents share a name (sub-agents), so a repo's own self-reviewer would otherwise replace the factory's. A checkout can still hold files under the factory-only names, because the repo is the factory itself or a branch added them. So a cell run that names one of the factory's agents passes the factory's own definition in the run's options. The Agent SDK ranks a definition passed that way above any .claude/agents/ file of the same name (Agent SDK subagents, "Filesystem-based definition"), so the self-review and address stages run the factory's reviewer and addresser whatever the checkout holds (PBI 96).
  • The PR reviewer only comments. Stage 8's reviewer is factory-pr-reviewer, passed in the run's options as the self-reviewer and addresser are, so a checkout's file of that name can't replace it. It reviews the one PR head its brief names against pr-review.md, says for each open thread in its brief whether that head settles it, and ends with APPROVED or OPEN: <n>. An answer the stage can't read gets one restate before the item asks a person: the stage asks the same reviewer session to give the same answer again in the required format, quoting why it couldn't be read, and runs no new review. A restated answer that reads carries on as a first answer would, and one still unreadable sends the item to NeedsInput with the restated answer's reason. The restate counts as no round and no attempt, and the stage logs it, so Run detail shows the reviewer needed a second ask (PBI 190). The repo host posts its findings as one review at that commit, with a body and line comments, and always with the COMMENT event. RepoHost.postReview takes no event at all, so the factory can't approve a PR or request changes on one, which keeps an agent out of every human slot. The repo host resolves a thread by its id, and resolving a resolved thread changes nothing (PBI 129). Posting a review returns the thread each line comment opened, so the stage tracks its own threads by id and never mistakes a person's thread for one of them. The cell's own GitHub token posts and resolves them, on its pull_requests write (PBI 128).
  • Trust. Policy files are code, reviewed like code. Every change under .factory/, to AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md, or under .claude/ needs a person. Agents follow them as the repo's instructions, while item text stays untrusted data.
  • Oversized items. The readiness judge also says whether an item is too big for one Sprint, as "oversized": true or false beside "flags" on its last line. A reply without it reads as false. Size alone never fails an item, since only the dor.md lines, the engine rules and the flags decide readiness. For an oversized item the factory asks the SOP's coding model, with no tools, for 2 to 4 child items. The request carries the same dor.md the judge read for the item, word for word: the repo's own, or the factory default when the repo has none. It asks for child bodies that meet every one of its criteria, so a child doesn't fail the checks it faces once the owner opts it in (PBI 202). Each child has a title, a body naming the parent and citing every spec section or plan task that child itself implements or changes, even one the parent's body doesn't cite (PBI 202), the indices of the parent's criteria it takes, and the earlier children it needs. The split is valid only when every parent criterion goes to exactly one child and each child names only earlier children as needs. A valid split goes on the parent as one comment, listing each child's title, its criteria word for word and what it needs, once per item text and split prompt. So a re-check for another reason, such as a dor.md change, posts no second proposal and files no second set of children, since the dor.md is in the request but not in that key (PBI 202), while a new split prompt posts one fresh proposal written from it (PBI 159). A split saved for filing, below, is never replaced, so a new prompt doesn't change it and its proposal isn't posted again. The factory then files each child as an issue in the parent's repo (PBI 144). The issue has the proposal's title, its body, and its criteria under the board's acceptance criteria heading. That heading holds the only criteria section in the body, and it lists the parent's criteria the split gave that child, word for word. The request tells the coding model to leave acceptance criteria out of each child's body, because the factory adds them. When a body still has its own section under that heading, at any level and in any letter case, the factory drops each such section up to the next heading and keeps the rest of the body. A body with no such section is filed whole (PBI 249). It's a sub-issue of the parent, sits on the parent's board in the backlog status, which is the status the field map gives Eligible, or NotReady when Eligible has none, and is blocked by the earlier children it needs. Each child carries the opt-in label from the moment it's filed, so the next poll takes it in as Eligible and the readiness gate judges it like any item. A child blocked by an earlier child waits in Queued until that child's issue closes. The owner withdraws a child by taking its label off, as for any item, and the factory never puts it back: a label goes on only when the factory files the issue, never on a child it finds already filed (PBI 237). A parent the factory filed itself, whose body carries a split marker, is the exception. Its children carry no label and wait for the owner, so a split can't keep splitting without a person looking. Once every child is filed, the parent gets one comment linking to each child and loses its opt-in label. The comment says the children carry the label and have entered the factory, and that removing a child's label withdraws that child, or, for a parent the factory filed, that none of them carries it, and the gate leaves it not ready. In the same commit the parent moves on from NotReady to Split through split_filed, so the next poll never finds it without its label and withdraws it to Abandoned, since its work went on in the children. A Split parent stays Split: its label coming back doesn't return it to Eligible, a change to a readiness input doesn't re-gate it, and the readiness judge is never asked about it again, so the parent itself never runs (PBI 225). Once every child the factory filed for the parent is Done, the next poll moves the parent from Split to Done through children_done. Before the move the factory posts one comment on the parent, listing each child with the PR that closed it, and closes the parent issue as completed. The children are the ones the parent's move to Split recorded, so a sub-issue a person added by hand doesn't hold the parent back. A child that's Failed or Abandoned, one that hasn't entered the factory, and one a person closed without it reaching Done all keep the parent Split, open and without that comment. A parent split before PBI 226 has no children recorded. For it the factory reads the parent's sub-issues and looks in the body of each one its own App opened for the split markers of a split it saved for that parent, newest first, so a child filed long ago is found however many issues the repo has had since, and takes the first split whose children it finds every one of. A sub-issue added by hand carries no marker, so it still doesn't count. A parent with no saved split, or with a filed child that's no longer among its sub-issues, stays Split (PBI 226). A parent split before PBI 225 lost its label once its split was filed, so a poll withdrew it to Abandoned. The next poll moves it from Abandoned to Split, once, when a split was kept for it and every child of that split is among its sub-issues by its split marker, and it then reaches Done like any Split parent. A parent with no kept split, or one missing a child of it, stays Abandoned (PBI 228). The parent's board status follows it to Split. On that move it gets the status the field map gives Split, once, so a status the owner sets later stands, and a field map with no status for Split, or a null one, leaves the board status as it was. The children keep their backlog status. The factory keeps the children it filed, in the order of the split, in the same commit that moves the parent to Split, so Floor and the parent's Run detail can show it as "Split into" (PBI 227). Filing is safe to repeat. The factory saves a valid split in the database, under the parent and its text, before it files any child, and files a saved split instead of asking the coding model again. A saved split is never replaced, so a filing that stopped partway is finished with the same children, after a restart too. Each child's body carries a marker for its parent and that parent's text, so a filing that stopped partway is finished on the next poll without filing any child twice. Only an issue the factory's own App opened counts as a filed child, so nobody else can plant a marker and stop a child from being filed. A parent that has any sub-issue this split didn't file, by hand or from an earlier text, is never split again. The factory checks that before posting the proposal, which says it files the children only when it will. A board whose field map gives Eligible and NotReady no status gets the proposal only. An invalid split posts no proposal, and the readiness comment, when there is one, says why a split couldn't be proposed. A coding-model run that fails or times out isn't an answer: the item stays Eligible, as it does after a failed judge run, and the next poll gates it and asks again (PBI 143). Before a new split is saved or filed, the readiness judge checks each proposed child, as the issue it would be filed as, against the same dor.md as the parent. A child that fails only dor.md lines gets one rewrite of its body from the coding model, given the dor.md and each failed line with the judge's reason, and is judged again. Its title, criteria and needs stay as proposed. A child that still fails, or that the judge flags, files no child of the split. The proposal comment then names, in that child's own section, each line it failed with the reason, and for a flag what the owner has to do, and says nothing was filed. A child the factory filed that later fails dor.md lines has its body rewritten once the same way. The factory keeps the body's acceptance criteria section and the line naming the parent word for word, edits the issue and gates it again at once, and that result stands. It edits only an issue its own App opened, whose body carries a split marker and that nobody has edited since, the App included, so a child is rewritten once. Any other issue is only commented on. A flag or a permission the App lacks is never rewritten, since only the owner can clear it, and the comment says what the owner has to do (PBI 264). My call
  • Changing a policy. When any file the readiness check reads changes on the default branch, meaning a policy file or config.yml, the factory re-runs the readiness check on every NotReady item. So a team that loosens a rule or fixes a broken file doesn't have to touch each item. A run already started keeps the files from its pinned commit. The readiness check also rests on the factory's own logic: the prompt it gives the judge, the prompt it gives the coding model to split an oversized item (PBI 159), and the engine rules no policy file can weaken. A change to any of them re-checks every NotReady item the same way, once, on the next poll after the factory restarts with it. A change to the judge's prompt or the split prompt counts by itself. A change to the engine rules counts when it raises the readiness version in the code (PBI 149).
  • Visible results. Run detail lists every criterion with its result and reason. Floor's not-ready strip shows the dor.md lines an item failed. The PR body carries the dod.md checklist with the cell's results, a link to pr-review.md, and the review rounds.

Repo config

Mechanical settings sit beside the policy files in .factory/config.yml, so they get reviewed and versioned like code. The factory reads them from the default branch when an item starts and pins that commit for the whole run. My call for pinning.

# .factory/config.yml, an example sensitive_paths: # each match needs at least one person - "infra/**" - "src/billing/**" reviewers: # used when the repo has no CODEOWNERS - your-org/payments-team web_tools: [] # agent web tools a cell may use: WebSearch, WebFetch bdd: # this repo's own runner commands parse: npm run bdd -- --dry-run run: npm run bdd report: reports/bdd.ndjson # Cucumber Messages, written by run commands: # what the SOP's cmd checks call setup: npm ci # optional: installs dependencies in each fresh checkout test: npm test lint: npm run lint failed_recheck_hours: 8 # optional: how often an item that failed on main is re-checked
  • Sensitive paths. A list of globs, empty by default, which owners can fill in once they know what needs protecting. Yours CI workflow files count as sensitive whatever the list says.
  • Web tools. web_tools lists the agent's web tools a cell may use, out of WebSearch and WebFetch, and is empty by default. WebSearch runs on Anthropic's side (Claude Code), so the egress proxy can't see what a search sends, and a steered agent could put data in a query. The agent's own deny list isn't enough to stop that, because an agent with a shell can call the model gateway directly and add the search tool to its own request. So the gateway enforces the list. It refuses a model request that asks for a server-side tool the run's list doesn't allow, an MCP server, or a URL for Anthropic to fetch (§9), and the agent is never offered a tool left out. WebFetch checks each hostname with api.anthropic.com before it fetches (Claude Code), and cells can't reach that host. Even with that check off, WebFetch reaches only the hosts on the egress allowlist, which a cell's shell reaches already, so turning it on adds nothing until the allowlist grows. The list lives under .factory/, so changing it always needs a person. Yours
  • Setup. A cell starts from a fresh clone with none of the repo's dependencies, so commands.setup, when set, runs once per cell after the base merge and before any stage. A failure blocks the run with the command's output, because every gate after it would fail for the same reason. A cell that resumes past Green runs no agent that would install anything itself. My call
  • Re-checking Failed items. failed_recheck_hours sets how many hours apart the factory re-checks an item that failed its Definition of Done on main, and it's 8 when the key is missing. Any number above zero counts. Unlike the rest of the file, the scheduler reads it from the default branch as it is now, at most every 10 minutes, since a Failed item has no run in flight to pin. A file it can't read, or a value that isn't a number above zero, counts as 8 (PBI 369). My call
  • Protecting the rules. Any change under .factory/, which holds this config and every policy file, always needs a person, whatever its tier. Without that, a factory PR could loosen the rules it gets checked against. My call
  • Trust lives outside the repo. Repo owners set whether the factory bot is a trusted author in the dashboard, not in this file. That way no PR can grant the bot trust. My call

The SOP lives in the factory's own repo, at sop/default.yml with its prompts under sop/prompts/. It has one entry per stage. The excerpt below shows the agent stages from Specify to Self-review. Checks named bdd and cmd run the commands in the repo's config, so the SOP names no language or tool. My call

sop: default version: 0.1.0 budget: # per PBI, across all stages usd: 40 wall_clock: 8h # runs only while the item holds a WIP slot models: # IDs live here, never in prompts coding: claude-opus-5-5 triage: claude-haiku-5-5 stages: - id: specify agent: planner model: coding prompt: sop/prompts/specify.md outputs: [features/**/*.feature, plan.md] exit: - every_criterion_has_scenario: true - bdd: parse # feature files load, steps listed retries: 1 on_fail: needs_input - id: sign-off approver: product_owner lock: features/**/*.feature - id: red agent: builder model: coding prompt: sop/prompts/red.md # step definitions and stubs, no behaviour exit: - bdd: fail_on_assertion # not undefined steps, not crashes - matches_lock: features/**/*.feature keep_output: true # red evidence for the Increment retries: 2 on_fail: needs_input - id: green agent: builder model: coding prompt: sop/prompts/tdd.md # red, green, refactor per unit exit: - bdd: pass - cmd: test # commands.test in the repo config - cmd: lint - matches_lock: features/**/*.feature retries: 3 timeout: 90m on_fail: retry - id: self-review agent: self-reviewer loop_until: "APPROVED" max_rebuttals: 2 # per finding, as in the table max_rounds: 5 # whole loop, findings or not on_fail: needs_input policy: .factory/ # dor, scenarios, pr-review, risk and dod; defaults in policy/

Phase 0 differs from the excerpt in two ways, both in plan Task 14. No cell ships a planner or builder agent, so those stages run the coding model with their prompt alone. And wall_clock counts each cell's own time from its start, because a clock across claims needs the control plane to keep it. My call

The $40 item cap is a starting figure, about twice the estimated cost per item in §11. Phase 0 measures real costs, and the cap gets reset from them. My call

07Concurrency

You wanted the number of items in flight to be configurable or worked out from past cadence. Yours The factory has three modes, set per factory:

ModeHow WIP is set
fixedA number in config, for example wip: 2.
adaptiveA formula, recomputed every hour over the last 14 days of history.
advisedThe formula sets the default, and a model proposes changes with written reasons. A proposal applies on its own only inside the formula's bounds. Outside them it waits for a human to approve it on the dashboard.

The adaptive formula

Little's Law says the average number of items in a stable system equals the arrival rate times the average time each spends inside, L = λW (Wikipedia). The factory's real limit is downstream, in how fast people review and accept its PRs. Starting more items than people can accept just grows the review queue, which breaks an anti-goal. So the rate in the formula is the human acceptance rate, and agent speed doesn't enter it.

demand = ceil(accept_rate × median_cycle_time) − max(0, review_queue − review_capacity) budget = floor(daily_budget ÷ median_cost_per_item × median_cycle_time) wip = min(clamp(demand, wip_min, wip_max), budget)

The clamp applies after the review-queue penalty, so wip_min stays the floor. The budget line applies last and can go below wip_min, down to 0, because money is a hard limit and WIP is not.

  • accept_rate. PBIs accepted per working day, last 14 days.
  • median_cycle_time. Working days an item holds a WIP slot, summed across its spells between InProgress and Accepted, same window. Time in Sign-off and Needs input is left out, because the item holds no slot there and Little's Law needs W to match what L counts. The budget line uses the same value.
  • review_queue. Factory PRs and scenario sign-offs waiting on a human right now. review_capacity is a config value, default 3.
  • Damping. WIP moves by at most 1 per hour. Lowering it only stops new starts and never kills a running cell. Raising it fills every new slot on the scheduler's next tick, up to the new limit and no further (PBI 177). A WIP override from the dashboard applies at once and skips the damping.
  • Cold start. Until 10 items have been accepted, the factory runs fixed at wip_min.
  • Usage limits. On a subscription, the five-hour and weekly limits bind before dollars do. When an agent hits one, its cell checkpoints and stops, and the scheduler starts nothing new until the reset time the limit message gives. Flow shows limit stalls next to the WIP line. My call
  • Usage reserve. Those limits are shared with your own Claude use, so the factory stops early. When a usage-limit event reports utilization at or above usage_reserve_at, default 0.7, the scheduler starts nothing new until the reset time, and items already running finish. My call
  • Waiting on people. The review_capacity brake in §5 applies in every mode, on top of the formula. The formula's own penalty only shapes the number between those bounds.

Formula first. A model choosing the number on its own can't be audited or reproduced, and that number sets the spend. The formula fits on one dashboard panel. The model still earns its place in advised mode, for things the formula can't see, like a holiday week or a release freeze noted in the backlog. My call

Sign-in accepts Google accounts, personal Microsoft accounts and work or school Microsoft accounts. Yours Signing in only proves who someone is. The dashboard's own allowlist decides whether they get in and what they can do. The whole team can read it, and a named few can use the controls. My call Setup details are in §11.

Overrides

You can override any decision the factory makes on its own from the dashboard. Yours An override outranks policy until someone clears it or it expires. The scheduler and the cells check active overrides at every decision point, so a change takes effect within 30 seconds. My call

ScopeDecisionOverride
FactoryRunningPause, resume or drain. Drain finishes the items in flight and starts nothing new. While the factory drains, Floor shows how many cells are still running, as "Draining: 2 cells still running", counted as Prepare restart counts them: an item counts when it's InProgress and its cell holds a live lease. Once no cell runs, Floor says the drain is done and it's safe to restart the factory or stop Docker (PBI 316).
FactoryRestartPrepare restart, before you restart the factory or stop Docker. Nothing starts, and every cell's lease renewal tells it to carry on, so it finishes the stage it's in. It then starts no further stage and ends its claim at that stage boundary, and the item waits in Queued at its next stage, with no attempt stopped and no work-in-progress commit (PBI 301). A pause, the kill switch or an operator's stop still tells a cell to stop. A cell stopped that way pushes its work in progress and reports its attempt stopped, which uses up none of the stage's retries. The factory never stops a cell itself, however long it runs, and no cell starts, even after current WIP is raised (PBI 300). Floor shows how many cells are still running, as "Preparing to restart: 2 cells still running", with no deadline. A cell whose lease ran out isn't counted. Once no cell runs, Floor says it's safe to restart (PBI 302). A starting control plane or worker clears the restart, and so does Resume. Each stopped item then carries on at the stage it was in, from the last commit it pushed.
FactoryWIPPin a number or switch mode. Approve or reject an advised-mode proposal. While a pin is active the formula keeps computing, and Flow shows the pinned and computed values side by side.
BacklogIntakePause one backlog or change its label filter.
ItemSelectionStart now, taking the next free slot ahead of backlog order. Hold, so the factory never picks it up. Move it up or down the factory queue without changing the backlog's own order. Re-queue a Failed or Abandoned item. Start now fits an Eligible, NotReady or Queued item, or one whose question was answered, and puts it ahead of every other item, answered ones and the final-stage group included. Move up and Move down fit a Queued or answered item, and move it one place among the items it's ordered with, which share its group and priority (PBI 320). A move is kept relative to the item's own board position, so a board reorder that shifts the item and its neighbours alike leaves the moved order as it was. A move also holds the item ahead of, or behind, the item it passed for as long as the board keeps those two in the order they had when the move was made, whatever else changes on the board, a new issue landing between them included. When a person puts the two in the other order on the board itself, the board wins: the move ends, the item follows the board, and Run detail says a change to the board's order ended it (PBI 311). None of the three gets an item past the readiness gate, a hold or an open blocker: a NotReady item marked Start now is claimed first once it passes readiness. Floor's "Next up" shares the claim order, so it shows each change at once (PBI 265).

  • Audit trail. Each override stores who set it, when, a required reason and an optional expiry. It shows as a badge on the item in Floor and Run detail. Quality reports override counts per SOP stage, so you can see which stages people keep correcting.
  • Expiry. An item override ends when the item reaches Done, Failed, Abandoned or Split. A factory or backlog override lasts until cleared or until its expiry, and the dashboard flags any that have been active for more than 24 hours. My call
  • Hard limits. No override crosses the git host's branch protection and required reviews, the monthly budget ceiling, the egress allowlist or the kill switch. Skipping a stage in the SOP never skips a check the git host enforces. Specify, Red, Green and Risk approval can't be skipped at all, so every Increment carries its scenarios, its red evidence and the approvals its tier requires. No override lowers a risk tier. My call
