Sprint Review. Your ssw-scrum:prepare-sprint-review skill already drafts Sprint Review emails from a GitHub project or an Azure DevOps board. As long as the factory keeps board status accurate, that skill covers factory work with no changes.

09Safety

  • Untrusted item text. Anyone who can edit a backlog item can plant instructions in it. Agents read item text as requirements to weigh and never as commands. The readiness gate flags items that ask for credentials, CI changes or access outside the repo. On a public repo anyone can also review a factory PR, so a review, and each review comment, steers the factory only when its author maps to an allowlisted user. Anyone else's review requeues nothing. The agent that addresses reviews is handed only trusted authors' comments, checked one by one, because a stranger can reply inside a thread an allowlisted user opened. It gets none of a thread the factory's own review opened, a person's reply in it included, since stage 8 checks and resolves those threads itself, and a review whose only text sits in such a thread requeues nothing (PBI 130).
  • Least privilege. One bot identity per backlog system, with access granted repo by repo and never org-wide. Phase 0 makes one exception, because it dogfoods on a personal account. GitHub documents Project access by GitHub Apps only for organizations, so the factory reaches a personal board with the owner's own gh CLI OAuth token, the owner's decision on 2026-11-06. That token can't be narrowed to the board: gh always asks for at least repo, read:org and gist, and the owner's token also holds admin:org, workflow and user. So in Phase 0 the control plane holds write on every repository the owner can reach, the owner's admin bypass of branch protection, and the power to edit CI workflows. Only the control plane holds it, and cells never see it. It has no expiry, and neither a new gh login nor gh auth logout revokes it, so the control plane's copy outlives both. Revoking it means revoking the GitHub CLI's access in GitHub's settings, which signs out every gh session. A project-only classic token was the narrower option the owner declined. Board edits show as the account owner. The App still does every repo action. Each cell gets a short-lived token for one repo and no production secrets, and never the owner's Claude token. A cell holds a stand-in for its own run and sends model calls to the control plane's model gateway, which checks the stand-in and swaps in the owner's token, so nothing a steered agent writes can carry it. The control plane mints the cell's GitHub token with an explicit permissions set: write on contents, pull_requests and issues, for item comments, and nothing on statuses or checks. Without that set the token gets "all of the permissions that were granted to the app" (GitHub), and a cell steered by planted item text could post a green risk-approval on its own PR. Only the control plane posts that check.
  • Platform-enforced protection. Branch protection and required reviews live in the git host's settings. A confused agent can't talk its way past them because no prompt controls them. The one check the factory posts itself, risk-approval, is pinned to the factory's App, and that App holds no admin or bypass rights (§6). A compromised control plane could still post a false green on that check. That residual risk is why the App's private key sits in Key Vault, where only the control plane's managed identity can read it. Phase 0's repo is public, which is what lets GitHub's Free plan give it branch protection and deployment environments with required reviewers (GitHub). main takes changes only through a PR with one approving review and a green lint check, so a cell's write on contents can't reach it. The owner, as admin, bypasses those rules, so they can merge their own PRs. The Azure deploy runs in a production environment whose required reviewer is the owner.
  • Network. An egress allowlist limits cells to the factory's control plane, the git host, the backlog API and package registries. Cells reach the model API only through the control plane's model gateway. Anthropic's servers can reach the web for a model request, through server-side tools or a URL in an image or document. So the gateway refuses both, except web search, which a repo turns on only by listing it in web_tools (§6). It checks the request it parsed and forwards that copy, so nothing it didn't read reaches the model. Locally the allowlist is an HTTP proxy on an internal Docker network, because the sandbox can't start there (§11).
  • Budget caps. Per item, per day and per month. The daily cap pauses new starts. The item cap sends the item to Needs input. So does the SOP's wall clock, which counts only time the item holds a WIP slot, so waits in Sign-off and Needs input don't use it up.
  • Kill switch. One dashboard button and one config flag. Either stops every cell within a minute.
  • Prepare restart. A dashboard control beside the kill switch, for a planned stop of the factory or Docker. Unlike the kill switch, it lets each cell wrap up first: nothing starts, every cell finishes the stage it's in and ends its claim at that stage boundary (PBI 301), and the cell API keeps answering so a cell can push and report. The factory never stops a cell itself, so each cell wraps up in its own time (PBI 300). It needs a reason and is logged like every override (§8).

10Failure and recovery

  • Checkpoints. The branch is the checkpoint. Each stage commits its output and the state store records the last stage completed. A new cell picks up from there. A cell stopped mid-stage, by a pause, the kill switch or an operator's stop, commits what its agent left and pushes it as work in progress, then reports the attempt stopped, which uses up none of the stage's retries. It pushes nothing when its lease was lost, since another cell may own the branch, or when the commit changed a locked feature file. The next cell resumes that stage on the branch at that commit and is told to carry on from the work there instead of starting over. A cell the launcher stopped resumes the same way, from its last pushed commit. An attempt the factory closed as stopped because its cell's lease ran out isn't resumed, and the next cell starts that stage over, unless the claim it ended was a restart's (PBI 239).
  • Stale branches. At every claim, before the next stage runs, the cell merges the base branch into the item's branch, because other items may have merged while this one waited. A conflict the agent can't resolve goes to Needs input. The cell fetches the base once per claim, and the check after the agent's pass merges that same commit again. Commits that land on the base while the agent works don't block the item: they reach the branch when the PR conflicts with its base and the item goes back to Queued (PBI 331).
  • Idempotent steps. Opening a PR, commenting and setting status each check current state before acting, so a retry never creates duplicates.
  • Retry budget. Set per stage in the SOP, plus a total per item. When it runs out, the item moves to Failed with a summary of every attempt.
  • Red main. When CI fails on a merge commit on main, the factory compares it with CI on the commit's first parent, the main commit it was merged onto. When a check failed that the first parent passed or never ran, the merge broke main. A check run that was cancelled proves nothing, as when a later push cancelled it, so a check cancelled on the first parent counts as one that never ran there. A merge whose own runs were cancelled and none failed broke nothing: it isn't charged, and it waits on main as below until a later main commit that contains it passes. The item moves to Failed, and the factory files one bug item with the opt-in label. The bug item names the merge commit, the PR and item it came from, each failed check with its URL, and the failing tests where the check's log names them. The scheduler claims it before anything else in the queue, so the factory fixes main before it builds anything more. When the first parent failed the same checks, main was already red and the merge isn't to blame. The item stays Accepted and waits on main, with no Definition of Done failure charged and no second bug item. Once CI passes on a main commit that contains its merge commit, it moves to Done. The one exception is the bug item of a break that still stands. Its merge is the fix for main, so when main is still red after it, the bug item moves to Failed rather than waiting behind itself. The break stays and no second bug item is filed. When main went red with no break the factory recorded, Floor still shows it red, with no item charged and no bug item. If an earlier merge whose CI hadn't reported yet turns out to have broken it, that merge takes the break over: it's charged and files its bug item. A break that has cleared before its bug item is filed, as when filing failed until a later commit on main passed, gets no bug item, since main is already green. While a break stands, Floor says main is red and names the commit that broke it and its bug item, until CI on a later main commit passes (PBI 255). Once that bug item has failed, Floor says main stays red until the bug item is re-queued or someone fixes it. These rules change, and a merge's CI can pass when it's run again, so a merge charged under older rules may not be charged today. #222 is one: it was charged before PBI 255, though its first parent 8d4fe69 failed the same ci check. So every failed_recheck_hours hours, 8 by default, the factory re-checks each item that went to Failed with dod_failed, counting from when it failed or was last re-checked. A re-check runs today's rules on the item's merge commit, the same ones an Accepted item gets. When they no longer say the merge broke main, because CI now passes on it, its only unpassed checks were cancelled, or main was already red, the item moves from Failed to Accepted with the event rechecked. Its board item gets one comment saying why, naming the merge commit and, when main was already red, its first parent. From Accepted it waits on main, or goes to Done, as above. When the rules still say the merge broke main, the item stays Failed, nothing is commented and no second bug item is filed, so a re-check that changes nothing makes no noise. Floor and Run detail show when each such item was last re-checked (PBI 369). My call
  • Quarantine. Three failures in a row on one repo pause that repo and raise a dashboard alert. A streak like that usually means a broken build or a bad SOP change, and the items themselves are fine.
  • Control plane restart. Leases and the event log live in Postgres, so a restart loses nothing. Cells keep running, and the scheduler finds them again through their lease renewals. A planned restart goes through Prepare restart first (§9), so every cell has wrapped up and no cell is running when the factory or Docker stops. Each cell ends its claim at the end of the stage it's in during the wrap-up, so the item goes back to Queued at its next stage (PBI 301). One stopped by a pause during the wrap-up ends its claim as it exits, even between a stage's end and its transition, so the item goes back to Queued at its stage. A starting control plane or worker clears the restart, and the restarted factory resumes each of those items, starting cells again up to current WIP.
  • New cell code on main. The worker keeps factory-cell:local current with main (PBI 210). As it starts, it records the checkout's HEAD as the commit it started at, since the control plane and the worker run the checkout's files and main is only fetched, never checked out. A worker restarted without a pull may run a commit behind main. It records that commit, with the label of the image the tag names and no restart asked for, before it fetches anything, so a start whose fetch fails still leaves a row that describes this run, and later polls measure main against the commit this worker runs. It then fetches main into the operator's checkout. When main changes no code the control plane or the worker runs compared with that start commit, it builds the image from main's commit. Otherwise it builds nothing, keeps the image there was, and Floor says a restart is needed and names main's commit. On each board poll it fetches main again. When every file changed since the commit it started at is cell-side (sop/, policy/, cell/, src/cell/, except sop/default.yml and src/cell/sop-move.ts, which the control plane and the worker load too, so a change to them needs a restart) or one no process runs (docs, feature files, tests, top-level Markdown), it rebuilds the image from main's newest commit, once, however many commits arrived. The control plane, the worker and every running cell carry on. A running cell keeps the image it started with, and the next cell started runs the new one. When any other file changed, shared code such as src/core/ included, it builds nothing, and Floor says a restart is needed and names main's newest commit, which a restart picks up. The build reads only the fetched commit, written from the checkout's object store into a temporary directory through an index of its own, so the checkout's working tree, index, branch and local commits never reach the image and never block it. Each image the worker builds carries the commit in its org.opencontainers.image.revision label. The start-up image the app host's cell-image resource builds from the checkout (PBI 206) carries HEAD's commit in the same label only when the working tree is clean, and no label when it has uncommitted edits, since that image was built from no commit. Whenever the worker builds nothing, because a restart is needed, or a build fails, it records the label of the image the tag names now, read with docker image inspect, as the commit the image was built from, or none when the image has no label. So Floor never names a commit from an earlier run, whose row Postgres keeps between runs. With no commit known, Floor says the image's commit is not known because it carries no commit label. Each rebuild logs a cell_image_rebuilt event naming the old and the new commit. A failed build keeps the image there was, logs a cell_image_build_failed event with the commit and the error, and is tried again on the next poll.
  • Network blips to GitHub. A cell reaches the outside world through the cell API, which often asks GitHub in turn, and through git push and git fetch against GitHub. One failed try of either no longer ends the attempt (PBI 259). When the cell API answers 5xx, or the connection is refused, reset or gets no answer within 90 seconds, the cell waits and sends the same request again, after 10, 20, 40 and 80 seconds, so 5 tries over 150 seconds. A push or fetch that fails on the network, on a proxy or GitHub 5xx, or on its 10-minute limit is retried the same way. A 4xx answer, such as the 400 for a commit that isn't on the run's branch, and a 409 for a lost lease are never retried, and nor is a git failure that isn't the network's, such as a rejected push. A call still failing after its tries ends the attempt as any other error does, and the attempt's message names the call and says it failed on a network or GitHub error after so many tries. When that call is the fetch of the claim's opening base merge, which runs before any stage, the cell opens an attempt of the stage the run resumes at to carry the message, unless the lease fence has fired. A cell that lost its lease, or failed to renew it 3 times, opens no attempt, since the control plane may be unreachable or another cell may own the run, and the claim ends on the fence's reason, such as the failed renewal, rather than on the network error. When GitHub answers the cell API 5xx or can't be reached, the cell API answers 503 with an error saying GitHub failed, and keeps 500 for its own faults, so the two can be told apart. Every request the factory sends to GitHub, from the cell API, the board client and the repo host alike, has a 30-second limit, and one that runs past it counts as GitHub failing, so a hung GitHub answers the cell 503 well inside its 90 seconds rather than leaving the call to time out. The lease renewal loop renews once a tick and keeps its own tolerance of 3 minutes of failed renewals. The lease fences the retries of a push or fetch: when the cell loses its lease, or fails to renew it 3 times, the retries end and a push or fetch still running is killed, because another cell may own the branch by then. A stop doesn't end them, since a stopped cell still pushes its work in progress. Each retry of a push, the push of work in progress included, checks the lease again first, as the first try does, so a cell that lost its lease while it waited pushes nothing.
  • Lost database connection. When Postgres ends a connection, because an administrator ended it, the server restarted or the network dropped it, the control plane logs it and keeps running. That holds for a connection lost while a transaction or the webhook holds it, as well as for an idle one: the work in flight fails and is logged, and the dead connection is dropped. The pool opens a fresh connection for the next query, so the next scheduler tick and board poll succeed once Postgres is back, and one that runs while it is down fails, is logged and is retried on the next run. The dashboard's live event stream ends its open streams, so each browser reconnects and listens again on a fresh connection.
  • Stuck transaction. A database transaction that never ends, such as one holding a lock it never releases, can stall the scheduler, the board poller or a cell's request to the cell API without an error, so nothing fails and nothing would be logged. Long-running work speaks up instead. A scheduler tick or a board poll still running after 5 minutes logs how long it has run and the step it is in, and logs again every 5 minutes until it ends. A cell API request still open after 60 seconds logs its route and run id. The warning only reports the stall. It doesn't cancel the work, so a person reading the log finds the stuck step and ends the transaction behind it. The factory logs rather than leaning on a database timeout, because statement_timeout and idle_in_transaction_session_timeout act through the backend's interrupt check, which a backend stuck this way never reached, so neither would have ended the stall.
  • Hung model call. An upstream model service can take a request and never answer it. The cell waits with no error, and the gateway holds no row lock, so the stuck-transaction warnings never see it. A model request whose upstream hasn't sent its response headers 60 seconds after the model gateway forwarded it logs its path and the same run id the cell API's slow line names, once, so a stuck model call looks different from a working agent. The gateway times only the wait for headers, because a healthy stream can run well past 60 seconds. The headers, an upstream error or the cell disconnecting end the watch, so a stream that started in time stays quiet however long it runs (PBI 154). Like the other warnings, it only reports the stall and cancels nothing.

Local run

Phase 0a runs the whole factory on the owner's machine before any Azure resource exists. An Aspire app host, apphost.mts, starts every dependency with aspire run. Yours for local-first, My call for the details below.

  • Dependencies. Postgres and the Azurite storage emulator run as Aspire container resources with data volumes. A container with the default lifetime is disposed of when the app host stops (aspire.dev), so the volumes are what let a restart keep every item, run and event. A one-shot migrate resource applies the schema and upserts the board and the dev owner. The control plane runs as a Node process and starts only after migrate exits, through the app host's waitForCompletion (aspire.dev). Secrets arrive as Aspire secret parameters, set from user secrets or Parameters__<name> environment variables with each dash written as an underscore (aspire.dev). The dashboard asks for any parameter with no value and can save it to user secrets. The one exception is the GitHub App key, which arrives as the path to its .pem, because the dashboard's one-line form drops a pasted key's line breaks (issue #207).
  • Start checks. Before any resource starts, the app host itself pulls and brings Docker up, so aspire run from the repo root is the one command that starts the factory (PBI 205, PBI 208). The npm run factory script that used to run these checks first is gone. On main it runs git pull --ff-only, so control, the worker and migrate run the code it pulled. A pull that fails, because main has diverged, local edits would be overwritten or the remote can't be reached, stops the start with git's own message, and no resource starts. On any other branch, or a detached commit, it warns that it runs the checkout as it is and pulls nothing. When docker version doesn't answer, it launches Docker Desktop and waits up to 3 minutes, asking again every 3 seconds, and stops with "Docker did not come up within 3 minutes." if it never answers. With Docker Desktop not installed where it looks, it stops with "Docker is not running, and Docker Desktop is not installed where this looks. Start Docker first." A test run, with FACTORY_FLOAT_PORTS=1 as the BDD suites start the app host, pulls nothing and runs no git, so a suite run on main never moves the checkout or waits on a credential prompt. It still checks Docker. aspire publish starts nothing, so it skips both checks.
  • Cell image at start. The egress proxy and every cell run factory-cell:local, so under aspire run the app host builds it itself, as a resource named cell-image in the Aspire dashboard (PBI 206). Like every resource it starts only after the start checks, so on main it builds the commit the pull brought in, and on any other branch the checkout as it is, uncommitted edits included. It runs docker build on the checkout with the checkout's own cell/Dockerfile, and labels the image with HEAD's commit only when git status --porcelain is empty. It builds on every start, even when an image is already there. The worker waits for cell-image to complete with exit code 0. A build that fails, Docker going away included, shows cell-image as failed with Docker's output in its console, leaves the image there was, and the worker never starts. Once the worker runs, it keeps the image current with main as the item above says.
  • Cells. The control plane starts each cell as a Docker container, from an image built for the machine's own architecture and never pushed. Cells reach the control plane and Azurite through Docker Desktop's host.docker.internal, so local upload URLs carry that host. The launcher gives a cell the model gateway's URL and a stand-in token for its run, never the owner's Claude token (§9). A Linux container keeps the cell's runtime and run: commands the same as in Azure. The sandbox is the exception: bubblewrap can't create a namespace in a cell container under Docker Desktop, so a sandboxed cell runs no Bash command at all. The owner chose to enforce the allowlist with the network instead. Cells join an internal Docker network, which "Containers on an internal network may communicate between each other, but not with any other network" describes (Docker). The same page adds that the network's gateway, and host services set up to listen there, stay reachable. A probe from an internal network found nothing answers there. Aspire's ports, bound to 127.0.0.1, refused the connection. Ports that other containers publish on every interface timed out. The egress test checks both kinds. A cell's one way out is a proxy container on that network and on the default bridge network, which admits only the allowlisted hosts plus the local control plane and storage emulator. The proxy lets through any request to the storage emulator that carries a SAS, so the emulator must not accept a SAS signed with Azurite's published devstoreaccount1 key. Under aspire run it runs on a random key that the app host draws at each start and hands to the control plane in FACTORY_BLOB, so a SAS a cell signs for itself gets 403 (PBI 84). Cells reach the proxy through HTTPS_PROXY, which Claude Code supports (Claude Code). The SDK sandbox stays off locally. A cell has no Docker daemon, so each test that needs a database starts its own Postgres server inside the cell, from binaries in the cell image. A cell runs the database suites and the @db scenarios as CI does. Scenarios that need the owner's machine, with Docker, Aspire and the real secrets, run in neither, so the owner runs them and the PR records the run.
  • Intake. GitHub can't reach a local machine, so the App's webhook stays off and the poller does all intake, closed PRs included. Sign-off and answers happen in the local dashboard, and comment commands wait for Azure's webhooks.
  • Sign-in. There is no built-in auth locally, and cells reach the same port. So the control plane prints a one-time sign-in link at each start, and only a browser holding the cookie it sets is the dev user. Every dashboard POST must come from the dashboard's own origin, the address the browser uses, locally and in Azure. Locally that's the address of Aspire's proxy in front of the control plane, which the app host passes in, not the port the control plane listens on behind it. The control plane refuses to start with a dev identity outside local mode, or inside any Azure container app. The app host sets local mode only for aspire run, and Azure never sets it.
  • App host language. The app host is TypeScript, like the rest of the repo. Aspire 13 scaffolds it with aspire init --language typescript (aspire.dev). The docs give it no stability label, so the first local run checked it, and it carried every resource above with no C# fallback needed (docs/superpowers/spikes/2026-11-local-platform.md).

How the factory runs on it:

  • No bare mode. Bare mode "does not read CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN" (GitHub Actions doc), so cells never run with --bare.
  • Test first. The Agent SDK docs don't say whether the SDK honours the OAuth token. Phase 0a checks it first, in a local cell container, and Phase 0b checks it again in Azure. If the SDK refuses it, cells drive the claude CLI headless instead, which documents the token.
  • Shared limits. The five-hour and weekly limits are "shared across Claude and Claude Code" (help center), so the factory and your own Claude use draw on the same allowance. §7 covers how the scheduler reacts when a limit hits.

Transcripts are large, so they go to blob storage and stage_run keeps a pointer. My call

Transcripts while a stage runs. A stage's transcript doesn't wait for the stage to end. While a stage runs, the cell uploads the transcript so far, every message its agent calls have written, to the attempt's usual path. It does so at most every 15 seconds, and only when new messages have arrived since the last upload that worked. Run detail links the transcript from the first upload, and the link shows everything up to the latest upload. Tokens and cost for a running stage stay 0 until the stage ends. When the stage ends, passed, failed or stopped, the cell waits for any upload still under way, then uploads the complete transcript to the same path. A failed upload while the stage runs is logged and skipped, and never fails or stops the stage. The next upload tries again, even with no new messages. A stage whose cell dies mid-run keeps its last upload, and Run detail shows that attempt as stopped, with the transcript as far as it got (PBI 209).

Every AI call records its cost. A cell's calls are charged to the stage attempt open at the time, and a cell call made while no stage is open is an error, so the model is never asked and no call goes unrecorded. The readiness gate runs before any run exists, so each of its AI calls, the judge's and the split proposal's for an oversized item, is a readiness_check row against the item, marked with which call it was. A call that fails on a usage limit, an API error or its timeout still records what it spent, and one that never started records a cost of nothing. Run detail lists an item's readiness checks next to its stages, and the Phase 0 report shows readiness spend across every item beside the stage spend, so the items the gate turned away count too (PBI 132).

plan: # Software Factory Phase 0 Implementation Plan > **For agentic workers.** REQUIRED SUB-SKILL: Use superpowers:subagent-driven-development (recommended) or superpowers:executing-plans to implement this plan task-by-task. Steps use checkbox (`- [ ]`) syntax for tracking. **Goal.** Build the Phase 0 walking skeleton from spec §13, in two stages. Phase 0a, Tasks 1 to 18, runs it on the owner's machine under Aspire. Phase 0b, Tasks 19 and 20, moves it to Azure. One personal GitHub repo, which is this repo, and one personal Project as its backlog, fixed WIP of 1, SOP stages 1 to 7 plus a thin stage 8 that addresses review feedback. The factory merges a PR once branch protection allows it and a person has ticked every `dod.md` line left for them (PBI 181), and the item reaches Done once CI on main is green. The risk classifier runs in shadow mode, and the dashboard has Floor with its four strips, Run detail and five overrides: pause, drain, stop a run, hold an item and re-queue one. **Architecture.** One TypeScript codebase with two entry points. The control plane runs the watcher, scheduler, dashboard and cell API in one process: a Node process under Aspire in Phase 0a, and a single always-on Container App in Phase 0b. A cell runs once per PBI, as a local Docker container in Phase 0a and a Container Apps job execution in Phase 0b, and drives the Claude Agent SDK through the SOP stages. Cells never touch Postgres. They talk to the control plane's cell API with a per-run token fenced by the lease generation. Postgres is the only state store, and every state change appends to the `event` table. **Tech Stack.** Node 26.13.0 LTS running `.ts` files directly through type stripping, `node:test`, TypeScript 7.0.2 for type checks only, `pg` 8.23.1, `yaml` 2.9.1, `@anthropic-ai/claude-agent-sdk` 0.3.318, `@octokit/app` 16.1.4, `@azure/identity` 4.14.1, `@azure/arm-appcontainers` 4.0.0, `@azure/storage-blob` 12.34.0, `@testcontainers/postgresql` 12.2.1, `@cucumber/cucumber` 13.3.0 for the Gherkin runner, `@types/node` 26.6.6 and `@types/pg` 8.23.1 for the type check, Bicep for infrastructure. **Spec.** `docs/superpowers/specs/2026-11-05-software-factory-design.html`, as revised on this plan's branch with the 14 flow-review fixes. §13's Phase 0 row is the scope. §14 lists the settled decisions this plan does not reopen. ## Global Constraints - Phase 0a runs locally. `aspire run` on `apphost.mts` starts: - Postgres; - the Azurite storage emulator; - a one-shot `migrate` resource; - the control plane as a Node process. Cells run as Docker containers that the control plane starts from `factory-cell:local`, built for the machine's own architecture and never pushed. GitHub can't reach the machine, so the poller does all intake. Sign-in is a dev identity that only `FACTORY_ENV=local` accepts. Postgres and Azurite keep their data in Aspire data volumes, so stopping `aspire run` loses nothing. Docker Desktop must be running. - Phase 0b, in Azure: region australiaeast. Control plane is one Container App at 0.5 vCPU and 1 GiB with external ingress. Cells are a Container Apps job, manual trigger, 2 vCPU and 4 GiB per replica, retry limit at least 1. - Azure images are `linux/amd64` and build in CI. No image built on the ARM64 dev machine is ever pushed. The local `factory-cell:local` image is the one native build, and it never leaves the machine. - In Azure, Postgres is a Flexible Server, Burstable B1ms, with Microsoft Entra authentication through managed identities and no stored password. - Transcripts go to Blob Storage, Hot LRS in Azure and Azurite locally, and `stage_run.transcript_ref` points at them. In Azure, container logs go to Log Analytics. - Key Vault holds the GitHub App private key and the Claude OAuth token in Azure, and Aspire secret parameters hold them locally. Cells never hold the Claude token. Each gets a stand-in for its run and sends model calls to the control plane's model gateway, which swaps in the real token (issue #33). Cells never run with `--bare`. - Model IDs live in the SOP file only: `coding: claude-opus-5-5`, `triage: claude-haiku-5-5`. - Phase 0 dogfoods: the target repo is this repo, `ricksu978/software-factory`, owned by a personal account, and the backlog is a Project on that same account. The GitHub App, installed on the account, does all repo work. The board is reached with the owner's `gh` CLI OAuth token, because GitHub documents Project access by GitHub Apps only for organizations. That token is far broader than the board, which spec §9 records as the owner's decision. Board edits therefore show as the account owner, and board changes arrive only through the 5-minute poll, since `projects_v2_item` webhooks are organization-only. This is a Phase 0 exception to spec §9's one-bot-identity rule, decided 2026-11-06. An org-owned board can replace it later without code changes, through the adapter's `owner` setting. - Eligibility label `factory`. Quality criteria live in the repo's policy files, per Run contract 11. A repo with no `.factory/dod.md` fails readiness for every item. - Poll every 5 minutes, on top of webhooks in Phase 0b. Leases renew every 60 seconds and expire after 5 missed renewals. A cell stops itself after 3 minutes of failed renewals. - `lease_generation` changes only as Run contract 2 says. A cell checks its generation before every push, comment and state write. - NeedsInput and SignOff items get reminders at day 2 and day 4, and move to Abandoned after 5 days with no answer. An operator re-queue or a late answer brings an Abandoned item back. - The scheduler starts nothing new while the waiting count (Run contract 3) reaches `review_capacity`, default 3, except an item at claim priority 1 (PBI 320), or while the last reported usage utilization is at or above `usage_reserve_at`, default 0.7. - The factory owns board status. The project's built-in status workflows are off, factory PRs reference their item with `Refs #n`, and the factory closes the item at Done. - Sign-off (`/approve`, `/changes <note>`) and answers (`/answer <text>`) are accepted in Run detail. In Phase 0b, once webhooks arrive, they are also accepted as item comments from GitHub logins mapped to allowlisted users. - An override takes effect within 30 seconds. The kill switch stops every cell within a minute. - Cell GitHub tokens are minted with explicit `permissions`: write on `contents`, `pull_requests` and `issues`, and nothing on `statuses` or `checks`. - Phase 0 runs WIP fixed at 1, SOP stages 1 to 7, a thin stage 8, and the risk classifier in shadow mode. The thin stage 8 runs `factory-pr-reviewer` on the factory's own PR before people look (PBI 128), and `pr-addresser` on the reviewer's findings, on requested changes and on merge conflicts. Shadow mode records a tier on every PR and posts no `risk-approval` check. - A merged item reaches Done once CI on main is green for the merge commit, so the target repo's CI runs its scenarios. Stage 10's post-merge verification, stage 11, budget caps, Inbox, Cost view and quarantine belong to Phase 1. - In Phase 0b, sign-in goes through Container Apps built-in auth with Microsoft (any Entra directory and personal accounts) and Google. Phase 0a uses the dev identity from Task 15. In both, the app's own `user` table decides access, and roles are viewer, operator and owner. - A cell has no Docker daemon, so it can't start a Testcontainers database. Test files that need a database use `dbTest` from `src/store/test-db.ts`, which skips them when `FACTORY_DB_TESTS=skip`, and scenarios that need one carry `@db` (Task 4). Until PBI 22, this repo's `.factory/dod.md` and `.factory/config.yml` set that variable and filtered `@db` out of `bdd.run`, so cells skipped both. PBI 22 gives every test its own Postgres inside the cell (below), and from then on `.factory/` sets neither, so a cell runs the database suites and the `@db` scenarios as CI does (Run contract 6). Scenarios that need the owner's machine carry `@local`, which cells and CI both skip (Task 4). - **A database in every test, inside the cell (PBI 22).** The cell image carries the Postgres 17 server binaries from the PostgreSQL apt repository, the version `startTestDb` uses in CI, with Debian's default `main` cluster turned off in `/etc/postgresql-common/createcluster.conf`. The image sets `FACTORY_PG_BIN` to `/usr/lib/postgresql/17/bin`, which isn't on `PATH`. With that variable set, `startTestDb` starts no container. It starts its own server instead, the same way Testcontainers gives each call its own (Task 4): - `initdb --auth=trust` in a fresh temp directory; - `pg_ctl start -w` with `listen_addresses=''` and `unix_socket_directories` set to that directory, so the server listens on no TCP port at all; - `stop` stops the server and deletes the directory. `initdb` refuses to run as root, and the cell runs as the non-root `factory` user that Task 14 Step 6 adds. The engine's `commandEnv` (Task 14) passes `FACTORY_PG_BIN` to every gate command, per Run contract 11. The variable names only a path inside the image, so it carries no secret. Run contract 5's cell env is unchanged, and Run contract 11's env for the gates' commands gains `FACTORY_PG_BIN`, because that env passes nothing else from the image. PBI 22 then drops `FACTORY_DB_TESTS=skip` and the `not @db` filter from `.factory/dod.md` and `.factory/config.yml`. An item with an `@db` scenario no longer fails Red with "not run in the cell". - **Two cells, or two test files in one cell.** Every `startTestDb` call has its own server, so nothing is shared: no rows, no database, no roles. A role a test creates, such as `id-factory-control`, dies with its server, as under Testcontainers. One shared server per cell would not do, because roles span a whole server and `migrate`'s advisory lock spans one database, so parallel files would race on `create role factory_app`. - **Who runs them.** The engine runs `commands.test`, `bdd.run` and every `dod.md` command itself, through `sh -c` outside the agent's sandbox (Run contract 11), so the gates always reach their servers. A test the agent runs from its own Bash may sit inside the sandbox where Azure turns it on, and Task 19 Step 9 checks whether it can still start a server there. - **The factory's own database.** Locally it is Aspire's `pg` container. A cell sits on the internal `factory-cells` network, and the egress proxy refuses every Postgres port (Task 13), so the cell can't reach it. In Azure the Flexible Server admits Azure services, which include the cell job, so a cell can reach it over the network. There the guard is authentication: the server takes Entra tokens only, the cell job carries only `id-factory-cell`, and that identity has no Postgres principal (Task 19). That is weaker wording than "can reach only its test database" in PBI 22's third criterion. Closing the network path too needs the server on a private VNet, which Phase 0 doesn't buy. - This repo is public, decided 2026-11-06. On the Free plan that's what makes branch protection and deployment environments with required reviewers available ([GitHub](https://docs.github.com/en/actions/how-tos/deploy/configure-and-manage-deployments/manage-environments)). `main` takes changes only through a PR with one approving review and a green `lint` check, and refuses force pushes and deletions. Admins bypass every one of those rules, because `enforce_admins` is off and "the restrictions of a branch protection rule do not apply to people with admin permissions" by default ([GitHub](https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/configuring-branches-and-merges-in-your-repository/managing-protected-branches/about-protected-branches)). That lets the owner merge their own PRs, which GitHub won't let them approve. The factory's App holds no admin or bypass rights, so a cell's push token can't write to `main`. Task 1 adds its CI job to the required checks, and Task 19 adds the `production` environment. ## Review Focus 1. **Planted instructions in PBI text.** An item body that asks for secrets, CI changes or access outside the repo is flagged NotReady by the gate, and no cell token can post a status or check. Tests in Task 9 and Task 7. 2. **Zombie cell after lease expiry.** An old cell whose lease was re-claimed gets 409 on every cell API write, so it can't push, comment or move state. Test in Task 12. 3. **Duplicate or replayed webhook deliveries.** The same `X-GitHub-Delivery` id processed twice yields one event. A bad or missing signature yields 401 and no event. Tests in Task 7. 4. **Spoofed identity headers.** A request that carries `X-MS-CLIENT-PRINCIPAL` on an auth-excluded path never authenticates a dashboard action, and an unknown signed-in subject gets the no-access page. Tests in Task 15, plus a live check in Task 19. 5. **Control plane restart mid-run.** A fresh scheduler process sees the running cell's live lease and starts no second cell for that item. Test in Task 13. ## Run contract These rules hold across every task. A task that touches one of them follows this section and does not restate it. 1. **Resume pointer.** `run.next_stage` names the stage the next cell runs, and the scheduler passes it to the cell as `RESUME_FROM`. These are its only writers: - `/stage` with `passed` sets it to the next stage in the pinned SOP; - a passed `specify` leaves it at `sign-off`, which no cell runs; - `decide` sets it to `red` on approve, and to `specify` on changes; - `changes_requested` sets it to `address`; - `pr_opened` sets it from `address` back to `open-pr`, where an InReview item's pointer stands, because the address run that sent it has finished its work (PBI 191); - `requeued` sets it to `open-pr` when `prState` reports the run's PR closed without a merge, so `openOrUpdatePr` opens a fresh PR from the kept branch; - a new run starts it at `understand`. 2. **Leases and generations.** `lease_generation` goes up by 1 exactly twice in a lease's life: when a claim moves an item into InProgress, and when any transition moves an item out of InProgress. The second bump fences the old cell, so its next cell API call gets 409. Leaving InProgress also clears `lease_owner` and `lease_expires`. `expireLeases` looks only at InProgress items. No other transition touches the generation. 3. **Waiting on people.** The waiting count is the number of SignOff and NeedsInput items whose question is still unanswered, plus every InReview item. Answered and Abandoned items don't count. The brake gates only claims that start new work: a Queued item with no open run, or whose open run has no `stage_run` row yet. Every other claim resumes work already in flight and is never gated. That covers an answered SignOff or NeedsInput item, and a Queued item back from `changes_requested`, `lease_expired`, `usage_limited` or a late answer. So answering never deadlocks the line, and an address run never waits behind the brake. 4. **Item scope.** Specify tags every feature file it writes with `@pbi-<externalId>` at Feature level. - `redGate` and `traceability` consider only scenarios carrying that tag. Among them, `redGate` needs a `@regression` scenario green rather than red (Task 10). - `greenGate` requires every scenario in the suite to be green, which keeps earlier items' scenarios as regression tests. - At sign-off, `run.locked_files` records the files carrying the tag, and `matchesLock` diffs only those files. So other items merged into the base never trip the lock. 5. **Cell context.** The cell's env holds only `RUN_ID`, `ITEM_ID`, `GENERATION`, `RUN_TOKEN`, `CONTROL_URL` and `RESUME_FROM`, plus the two model variables from `cellModelEnv` in `src/control/model-gateway.ts`. The scheduler passes the six. `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` points at the control plane's model gateway, `<CONTROL_URL>/internal/model`, and `CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN` holds a stand-in, `sk-ant-oat01-<runId>.<generation>.<runToken>`, never the owner's token (issue #33). The gateway checks the stand-in the way the cell API checks a run token, so a leaked stand-in reaches only the gateway's allowlisted model paths and dies with the run's generation. In Azure the gateway is on public ingress, so until then it works from anywhere. Locally `dockerLauncher` also adds the egress variables from Task 13: the proxy variables and `NO_PROXY` in both cases, `NODE_USE_ENV_PROXY`, `CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_NONESSENTIAL_TRAFFIC` and `ENABLE_CLAUDEAI_MCP_SERVERS`. None of them carries a secret. Everything else comes from `GET /internal/cells/:runId/context`: - the item's external id, title and acceptance criteria; - `nextStage`; - the latest decision or answer, with its note; - `lockSha` and `lockedFiles`; - `prNumber`, `repo`, `base` and `branch`; - `configSha` and `sopVersion`; - `dodVerdicts`, the latest `dod.md` verdicts from `policy_result`, so a cell resumed at open-pr still gives the classifier the `person` lines, and `dodCheckedSha`, the commit they were checked at; - `scenarioNotes`, from `run.scenario_notes`, the approving self-review round's `SCENARIO NOTE:` lines, so an open-pr in a later claim, after a usage limit, a stop, an answered block or a requeue, still writes them into the PR body (PBI 152); - `trustedComments`, for an address run, under Run contract 10; - `trustedBot`, the repo's `trusted_bot`, so the PR review stage can tell the factory's own threads and reviews on the PR from people's (PBI 318); - `stageAttempts`, the highest attempt in `stage_run` per stage, so a later claim on the same run numbers its attempts on from there and writes over no earlier row or blob; - `resume`, which is `{ stageId, attempt }` when the last attempt at `nextStage` is `stopped`, and null otherwise (PBI 140). The cell then carries on from the work in progress that attempt pushed. An attempt the factory closed as `stopped` because its cell's lease ran out, whose message is `LEASE_RAN_OUT` (PBI 239), gets no `resume`: no stop cut it short and it may have pushed nothing, or a half-finished commit, so the next cell starts that stage fresh, as it did when such an attempt stayed `started`. The exception is a claim a restart ended, through `releaseForRestart` or, before PBI 300, the scheduler's stop at the end of the wrap-up: when the `lease_expired` event that ended the attempt's own claim, the item's first one at or after the attempt's `started_at`, has `reason: "restart"`, its attempt still resumes, as PBI 140 has it. A later claim's `lease_expired` says nothing about the attempt, since that claim's cell may have opened no attempt at the stage. 6. **CI status.** Only the control plane reads checks, with the App's own `RepoHost`. The cell reports its PR through `POST /pr` as soon as the PR exists. After every push, the cell asks about the exact commit it pushed with `GET /internal/cells/:runId/checks?sha=<sha>`. The control plane polls the checks on each sha it has been asked about, and on every merge commit. A sha with no checks reported 10 minutes after the control plane first saw it returns `none`. A sha CI failed on returns each failed check's name and URL, and the last 100 lines of the log of each of the first 5 (`LOGGED_CHECKS`), read by the control plane, so the cell learns why CI failed without GitHub access (PBI 232). Later failed checks have a null log. Each log line is cut at 500 characters, ending in "…", and the oldest lines go once the tail passes 20,000 characters, so a test that dumps a large blob can't swell the finding. The engine treats `none` as `blocked`, with "no CI ran on the PR". The cell waits at most 60 minutes for CI on any one commit, counted from when that wait began in the cell. A cell claimed again or restarted on the same head starts a fresh 60 minutes, since the cap counts per wait, not from `check_watch.first_asked_at`. CI still `pending` then is `blocked` too, with a question naming each check still pending, from `GET /internal/cells/:runId/pending-checks?sha=<sha>`. Pending CI isn't failed CI, so a timeout never goes back to green or counts against a retry (PBI 234). A `dod.md` line that names a CI check reads the checks by name through `GET /internal/cells/:runId/ci-checks?sha=<sha>` in the same way (PBI 229). Phase 0 requires CI on the target repo. Cell tokens keep the permissions in Global Constraints. The cell's own repo calls go through `cellRepoHost`, which opens PRs and requests reviewers with the token from `/github-token`. 7. **Branches and runs.** A run's branch is `factory/pbi-<externalId>-r<runNumber>`. These start a new run on a new branch from the base: - `criteria_changed`; - a re-queue of an item whose PR already merged. The previous PR, if still open, is closed with a comment that names the kept branch. 8. **Board mirroring.** Every committed transition and override is mirrored onto the item's board. Since PBI 219 the worker does it from the event's board mirror outbox row, not from a hook in the process that made the change. - It writes `fieldMap.statusFor[to]` through `setStatus`. A null entry leaves the board's status as it is. A move to Split writes `splitStatus(fieldMap)` from `src/control/board.ts`, which is `statusFor.Split`, or nothing when that entry is missing, null or empty. A parent moves to Split once, so its board status is set once and a status the owner sets after stands (PBI 227). - It calls `claim` on every move into InProgress, which is idempotent, so a revived item gets its marker back. It calls `release` on reaching Done, Failed or Abandoned, and `linkPr` on `pr_opened`. - It closes the item at Done. - Whenever an item with an open PR reaches Abandoned, through `withdrawn` from any state, the PR is closed with a comment that names the kept branch. The poller already closes it when it withdraws an item (Task 8), so the hook skips a PR that's no longer open. 9. **End-of-stage order.** A stage ends with these calls in this order: `/stage` with `passed`, then every `/upload-url` upload, then `/pr` when the stage opened a PR, and the `/transition` last. The transition is the call that raises the generation, so any call after it would get 409. A stopped attempt (PBI 140) sends its uploads first and `/stage` with `stopped` last, because during a restart that report ends the claim and raises the generation too. Its row already exists from its `started` report. 10. **Review triggers.** Requested changes count only when a review from an allowlisted login was submitted after `run.reviews_seen_at` and either requests changes or leaves a comment in a thread that is still unresolved. The second case covers a review that only comments, such as the PR reviewer's, whose findings are inline threads. A resolved thread asks for nothing. A thread the factory's own review opened, whose first comment is by the repo's `trusted_bot` as `botKey` names it, asks for nothing either, whoever replies inside it: it belongs to the pr-review stage, which checks and resolves it itself. The poller passes the repo's `trusted_bot` to `prState`, which skips those threads (PBI 130). For the same reason a review that requests changes counts only when it has a summary or a comment outside the factory's threads. One whose only text is a reply inside a factory thread would hand the address run nothing to read. `prState` matches each thread comment to its review by the review's `databaseId` (PBI 130). Only a comment in a thread that is unresolved when the poller reads it gives such a review its text. So whether a thread sends the item back depends only on whether it is resolved at that moment, never on what its comments say: a resolved "Not fixed" sends nothing back, and an unresolved "Verified, fixed." does. An approval asks for nothing, even with a summary (PBI 258). Each `changes_requested` move names its cause in its transition payload's `cause`: `{ kind: "thread_comment", threadId, author, body, submittedAt }` for a comment in an unresolved thread, `{ kind: "review", author, body, submittedAt }` for a review's summary, or `{ kind: "not_mergeable" }` when GitHub reported the PR not mergeable and no newer trusted text waits. With several waiting, the newest names it. `prState` returns it as `lastChangesRequested`, and the webhook names the review it was delivered (PBI 258). A thread comment counts only once it has stood two minutes. A reviewer posts a verdict reply and then resolves the thread, and a poll between the two would send the item to address with nothing left to read. Past those two minutes, any trusted reply on an open thread counts as a new review, so a "thanks" left open starts one more address run. A thread whose only trusted comments predate the last address claim never fires again, so a reviewer who still finds it unfixed has to reply in it or review again. Two writes set that column: - `POST /pr`, when the cell records the PR in the open-pr stage. A retried open-pr attempt records it again and keeps the clock. The PR is open on GitHub while the factory's own PR review runs and the item is still InProgress, so a trusted review left then counts, and it sends the item to address on the first poll after the item reaches InReview (PBI 191). A `pr_opened` with no `POST /pr` before it starts the clock instead; - the claim that starts an address run, set to that claim's time. A review left while address is running is newer than the claim, so the next poll still catches it once the item is back in InReview. The webhook compares a changes-requested review's `submitted_at`, and only for a review with a non-empty summary. Its payload carries no line comments, so it can't tell whether a review with no summary holds anything outside the factory's threads, and leaves that review to the poll (PBI 130). The poll compares the newest such review from `prState`, which reads each open thread comment's review time over GraphQL, so only the poll catches a review that only comments. GitHub's aggregate `reviewDecision` isn't used, because it can stay `CHANGES_REQUESTED` after the fix is pushed. **Trusted reviewers.** The repo is public, and "Anyone with read access can review and comment on proposed changes" ([GitHub](https://docs.github.com/en/pull-requests/collaborating-with-pull-requests/reviewing-changes-in-pull-requests/about-pull-request-reviews)). So a review, and each review comment, counts only when its author's login is the `github_login` of an allowlisted user, the same rule item comments follow. Trust is per comment, because anyone can reply inside a thread a trusted reviewer opened. An untrusted review requeues nothing. `GET /context` gives an address run `trustedComments`, the comments in unresolved threads written by trusted authors or by the App's own bot user, with their thread, path, line and body. A thread the factory's own review opened is left out whole, a trusted reply inside it included, through `withoutFactoryThreads` in `src/adapters/types.ts` (PBI 130). A reviewer can also request changes with only a top-level summary. A summary can't be resolved, so it joins the list while its author's latest review, not counting reviews that only comment, requests changes, as in GitHub's own reviewer state. It has the review's id as its thread and no path or line, and the same author rule applies to it (issue #28). Logins match as GitHub compares them, ignoring case, through `loginKey` in `src/adapters/types.ts`. GraphQL names a bot without the `[bot]` suffix REST adds, so the GitHub adapter asks for each author's `__typename` and names a `Bot` author `name[bot]`. `botKey` gives the repo's `trusted_bot` the suffix when it was stored without one. So a user account with the bot's bare name never matches the bot. Whole keys are compared, so a login that only starts with a trusted one never matches either (issue #79). Nothing marks a summary answered, so it comes back in every address round until its reviewer approves or reviews again, and the addresser's PR comment answering it doesn't come back with it. The address prompt says so: a standing summary may already be dealt with, so the addresser checks the code before changing anything for it. The bot's comments are the addresser's earlier replies. They came from a brief that held only trusted text, and without them a second round would see a reviewer's follow-up but not the reply it answers. The engine gives the addresser that list and nothing else from the PR, so an untrusted comment never reaches its brief. 11. **Policy files.** The factory hard-codes no quality criteria. Spec §6 "Policy files" defines five files: `dor.md`, `scenarios.md`, `pr-review.md`, `risk.md` and `dod.md`. - **Loading.** The factory reads them from the repo's `.factory/` at the run's pinned `config_sha`. Readiness has no run yet, so it reads the default branch head. A read that returns 404 means the file is absent. Any other read error throws, and the step retries on its next turn. A read error never falls back to a default. - **Defaults.** An absent file falls back to `$FACTORY_POLICY_DIR/<name>.md`, except `dod.md`, which has no default. A `Policy.sha` is the SHA-256 of its raw text, whether it came from the repo or a default, so a changed default counts as a policy change. Both images copy the factory's `policy/` folder to `/app/policy`, which is the default value of `FACTORY_POLICY_DIR`. A repo file replaces its default whole. The worker's poller reads the defaults another way (PBI 261): `loadPolicy` takes an optional `DefaultPolicies` reader, and the worker passes `mainDefaults` from `src/worker/main-defaults.ts`, which reads `policy/<name>.md` with `git cat-file blob` at the checkout's `refs/remotes/origin/main`, the commit the cell image loop last fetched. The fingerprint and the gate's criteria both come from it, read once per poll, so an uncommitted edit or a local commit in the checkout never counts, and a failed fetch leaves the defaults at the commit last fetched. Cells pass no reader and read their image's `/app/policy`. - **Criteria.** Only `dor.md`, `pr-review.md` and `dod.md` have criteria, one per top-level `- [ ]` line, numbered from 1 in file order. The judge answers one JSON line per criterion: `{"index","status","reason"}`, where `status` is `passed`, `failed` or, in `dod.md` only, `person`. `person` means the line can only be met by a person or after merge, such as "deployed to staging". It goes to the PR checklist unticked and never counts as a fail. A missing index fails, and when an index appears twice, a fail wins. `scenarios.md` and `risk.md` are guidance, given whole to the agent that uses them. - **Commands.** A criterion holding `` `run: <command>` `` is allowed only in `dod.md`. `loadPolicy` rejects it in any other file with `PolicyError`. The cell runs `dod.md` commands at the end of green, in the checkout, as `execFile("sh", ["-c", command], { cwd, timeout: 900_000, env: { PATH, HOME, CI: "true", FACTORY_PG_BIN, ...proxy } })`, where `proxy` is the four proxy variables and `NO_PROXY` in both cases when the cell has them (Run contract 5). `FACTORY_PG_BIN` is the image's path to the Postgres binaries, so `startTestDb` can start a server in the command (PBI 22, Global Constraints). It is passed only when the image sets it. Without the proxy variables a command that needs the network, such as `npm ci`, fails locally. That env carries none of the cell's tokens. It isn't a sandbox, though: the command runs as the cell's own user, as `commands.test` does and as the agent does. So it has no more reach than the agent that wrote the code already has. The `bdd.*` and `commands.*` lines in `config.yml` run the same way, through `sh -c` in the checkout, so they may use shell syntax such as `VAR=value` and `$(...)`. A cell's clone has none of the repo's dependencies, so `commands.setup`, when set, runs once per cell after the base merge and before any stage, and a non-zero exit blocks the run with its output. This repo's is `npm ci`. Without it, a cell that resumes past green runs its first gate command with nothing installed. - **CI checks (PBI 229).** A `dod.md` criterion may also hold `` `ci: <check name>` ``, which `parseCriteria` reads into `Criterion.ci`, and `loadPolicy` rejects it outside `dod.md` with `PolicyError`, as it does `run:`. `checkDefinitionOfDone` in `src/cell/engine.ts` asks `ciChecks(head)` once, only when some line names a check, and only when the item has a PR, through the cell API's `GET /ci-checks?sha=`. A line whose check passed on `head` passes with the reason `CI check "<name>" passed: <url>`, and one whose check failed fails with `CI check "<name>" failed: <url>`. Neither runs its command. Only an exact name on `head` counts. A run of the check that failed fails the line even when another run passed, and a run still in progress gives no verdict. A line whose check gives no verdict, because there is no PR, CI hasn't reported on `head`, or the check is still running, is checked as before: its command runs, or the judge decides it. When CI reported on `head` but not under the line's check name, the line falls back the same way, and the check's findings carry `the CI check "<name>" that Definition of Done line <n> names was missing on <sha>`. A missing check fails nothing alone, so the engine adds that note to the attempt's `/stage` message, and the stage fails only on failed lines. This repo's `dod.md` line 1 names its `ci` job. - **Base failures (PBI 215).** A `run:` line that fails is run again, before the failure counts against the item, on the run's base commit, `origin/<base>` as the claim's merge fetched it. `runOnBase` in `src/cell/base-run.ts` runs it in a temporary `git worktree` at that commit, after `commands.setup` when set, through the same `sh`, then removes the worktree, so the item's checkout and branch stay as they were. It makes no agent call, runs only after a line failed, and runs each command at most once per cell. `failingTests` reads the failing tests' names from the whole output: TAP's `not ok` lines, node's spec reporter's `✖` lines and, from cucumber-js 13.3.0, each `N) <name> # <path>:<line>` entry of its "Failed scenarios:" block, skipping the indented step and error lines under each, up to the `N scenarios (...)` summary. When every test that failed on the item's branch also fails on the base, and at least one was named, the base is at fault. The verdicts are stored as usual, then the check throws `BaseFails`, a kind of block, so green, address or open-pr don't retry. The item moves to NeedsInput with one question that says the base fails in the cell and names the base commit, each such line and its tests, and that the item isn't at fault. The question carries `baseFailure: { sha, tests, base }`, with `base` the run's base branch, which the poller watches for green CI (PBI 260). Before the transition, `finish` calls `pushWorkInProgress`, which commits what the attempt left, checks the lease with `api.lease()`, and pushes, so work Green committed but hadn't pushed is on the branch the next cell clones. A lease check that throws pushes nothing, and a commit that changed a locked feature file isn't pushed, as in the stop's wrap-up. `pushWorkInProgress` reports whether the push went through, and the question says the work is pushed and the stage runs again on it only then. Otherwise it says the branch holds only what was pushed before. The attempt still ends and the item still moves to NeedsInput either way. A failure the base doesn't share, a test that fails only on the branch, or output that names no test, counts against the item as before, with retries. So does a base run that throws, such as a missing `origin/<base>` or a worktree that can't be added: the engine logs the error and treats the base as sharing no failing test, so the cell carries on instead of ending. - **CI failures go back to Green (PBI 292).** `src/cell/ci-failure.ts` holds the pieces. When CI fails on a head open-pr, address or pr-review's fix pushed, `ciFailed` reads `GET /ci-checks` on it into a `CiFailure`, `{ sha, checks: { name, url, failingTests }[] }`, with only the failed checks, and `ciFindings` gives Green one finding per check, naming the commit, the check, its URL and its failing tests, or saying CI named none. When every failed check names failing tests, the cell first reads `GET /ci-checks?sha=<base>&on=base` on `origin/<base>`, and `sharedCiLines` blames the base when the base's failed checks fail each of those tests: the stage throws `BaseFails` with the checks as lines, so `baseQuestion` names each check with its URL, and Green never runs. Address takes its head before the addresser's call. When CI fails on a fix the addresser committed, address retries with the findings, as before. When the addresser committed nothing, as when it only replied, address has no agent work left to change the head, so it doesn't retry on it: it posts its replies, ends its attempt as failed, and returns the findings, so the run goes back to Green. The cell keeps each head CI failed on, and `readCi` never reads CI on one again. Green's next attempt is reported to `/stage` with `ciFailure`. A Green pass whose head is still the failed commit after its agent call throws a block with `ciQuestion`, which names each failed check with its URL and failing tests, each commit CI failed on, how many times Green tried and that the last attempt left the commit unchanged, so the item moves to NeedsInput instead of Failed. Green running out of retries still fails the item, as PBI 128 has it. An address retry whose head is one CI already failed on goes back to Green without reading CI again. - **Fresh DoD.** Self-review and address can push code after green, and CI may not run a `run:` line such as `run: npm run e2e`. So each `dod.md` verdict records the commit it was checked at, in `policy_result.checked_sha`. Open-pr, and address before it posts `pr_opened`, check `dod.md` again whenever `git.head()` differs from `ctx.dodCheckedSha`, or the verdicts at that commit hold a failed line, so a retry that leaves HEAD where it was still gets checked. A failed line found there sends open-pr back to green, counted against green's retries, and counts as a failed address attempt. The PR checklist names the commit its verdicts were checked at. - **Results.** Every result is stored in `policy_result`, with `source` set to `repo` or `default`. The control plane writes readiness rows itself, and the cell sends its rows through `POST /policy-results` (Task 12). - **Re-gating.** `readinessSha(texts)` (Task 9) is the SHA-256 over every file the readiness check reads: the five policy files and `.factory/config.yml`. Each file contributes its raw text as read, or the default's text when the repo has none, prefixed with its length in UTF-8 bytes and a colon, so no text can slide across into the next file. A missing `dod.md` or `config.yml` contributes `-;`, which no length prefix starts with, so it never matches a file holding the word `absent` (PBI 21). Raw text means a file that fails to load, such as a `pr-review.md` with a `run:` line, still counts, and fixing it changes the hash. `item.readiness_policy_sha` records the value from the item's last check. The factory's own readiness logic follows the six files, length-prefixed the same way: the judge's prompt, which is `judgePrompt`'s words around an empty item and a `dor.md` with no text and one empty criterion, so the per-criterion line counts too, `READINESS_VERSION` from `src/policy/policy.ts`, and the split prompt, which is `splitPrompt`'s words around an empty item with one empty criterion and `TEMPLATE_DOR`, the same stand-in `dor.md` with no text and one empty criterion (PBI 159, PBI 202). Raise that version by one with any change to the engine rules (PBI 149). When the sha changes, because a team fixed any of those files, a change to a default merged to `main` and fetched by the worker (PBI 261), or a deploy changed the judge's prompt or the split prompt or raised the version, the poller re-runs the gate on the item. An item in a repo the factory doesn't know gets a sha over the logic alone, so a logic change re-checks it too. - **Engine rules.** The rules no policy file can weaken are the list under "What stays in the engine" in spec §6. They live in code and prompts that the factory owns. 12. **Network retries (PBI 259).** `withRetries` in `src/cell/retry.ts` tries a call again after 10, 20, 40 and 80 seconds (`RETRY_WAITS_MS`) while the failure is transient, then throws `NetworkError`, whose message is `<call> failed on a network or GitHub error after <n> tries: <last error>`. Any other failure is thrown at once. - **Cell API calls.** `httpCellApi` retries every call on a 5xx answer or a fetch that rejects, which covers a refused or reset connection and a try with no answer within `CALL_TIMEOUT_MS`, 90 seconds. Each try sends the same request. A 409 is `LeaseLost` at once, and any other 4xx fails at once with its status and body, as before. The blob `PUT` of an upload isn't a cell API call and isn't retried. `lease({ once: true })` tries once: the engine's renewal loop uses it, so its tolerance of 3 failed renewals stays 3 minutes. The lease check before a push or a transition retries like any call. - **git.** `shellGit` runs `push` and `fetch` with a 10-minute limit (`REMOTE_TIMEOUT_MS`) and retries them when `gitNetworkFault` holds: the command was killed by its limit, or its stderr shows a host that can't be resolved or reached, a reset, refused or timed-out connection, an early EOF, or a 5xx from GitHub or a proxy. A rejected push, a 4xx and a missing ref aren't retried. A base merge that throws, a fetch out of retries included, opens an attempt of the run's `nextStage` before `finish` ends it failed, so the attempt's message says why. The one exception is a fenced cell: when `fence.signal` has aborted, the merge's catch opens no attempt and rethrows `fence.signal.reason`, such as `RenewalFailed`, so `finish` acts on the fence and makes no further control-plane calls. The clone in `src/cell/main.ts` isn't retried. - **The lease fence.** `withRetries` takes a `RetryFence`, `{ signal?, beforeRetry? }`. An aborted `signal` ends the loop with its reason, before a try, during the wait or mid-try, where `shellGit` passes it to `execFile` so the git child is killed. `beforeRetry` runs before every try after the first, and its throw ends the loop. The engine keeps a `fence` `AbortController` apart from the stop's, aborted only when the renewal loop gets `LeaseLost` or gives up after 3 failed renewals, never by a stop, because a stopped cell still pushes its work in progress. Every `push` and the base merge's `fetch` take `fence.signal`, so a cell fenced off while it waits to retry pushes nothing more, since another cell may own the branch by then. A stage's push passes the engine's lease `guard` as `beforeRetry`, and the push of work in progress passes `api.lease()`, so a lease check is one command before every push try, retries included. - **The cell API.** A route that throws Octokit's error for GitHub answering 5xx, or for a request to GitHub that got no answer (status 500, or an `AbortError`), answers 503 with `{ error: "GitHub failed: <message>" }`, through `githubFailed` in `src/adapters/github/errors.ts`. A GitHub 4xx and the cell API's own faults still answer 500. - **The GitHub time limit.** Every Octokit client the factory builds for GitHub is `TimedOctokit` from `src/adapters/github/timed.ts`, whose `fetch` aborts a request after `GITHUB_REQUEST_TIMEOUT_MS`, 30 seconds. That covers the Apps that the cell API, the control plane (`src/main.ts`) and the worker (`src/worker/main.ts`) build, so every installation client they make, and with it `githubRepoHost` and the board client on an org board; `githubBacklog`'s board client on the project token; and `cellRepoHost`. Octokit turns the abort into its error with status 500, so the cell API answers 503 well inside the cell's 90 seconds, and the cell retries. Without the limit a hung GitHub fails only after undici's 300 seconds, so the cell gives up on the call first and the hung handler holds the run's row lock. --- ## File structure ``` package.json,
